title: Read the signature, then the return, then the middle
description: A generated diff lands in front of you with no explanation. Reading top to bottom wastes the fastest information you have: what goes in, what comes out, and only then how it gets there.

learningObjectives.text: Read a function's signature and return statement(s) before its body to form a testable hypothesis about its purpose
Use that hypothesis to read the body as a check rather than an open-ended search

contentSections.title: Signature first

contentSections.body:
A pull request lands on your desk. It's a Claude Code diff, no description beyond the ticket number. The new function:

```python
def reconcile_ledger(entries: list[dict], as_of: date) -> ReconciliationResult:
```

You haven't read a single line of the body yet, and you already know more than it looks like. `entries: list[dict]` and `as_of: date` in, a `ReconciliationResult` out — not a bool, not a list, a named result type. That's three real facts about what this function is for, sitting in one line, before you've spent a second reading logic.

Most people read code top to bottom, the order it's written in — which is also the order that's slowest to give you the information you actually need. The signature and the return statement carry disproportionately more of a function's *intent* than its middle does, because they're the interface: what it promises to accept and what it promises to hand back. The middle is just the mechanism for keeping that promise.

Read in this order instead: signature, then every `return` in the function (there may be more than one — each one is a distinct way the function can conclude), then the body. By the time you reach the body you're not reading to discover what the function does, you're reading to check whether the mechanism actually delivers what the signature and returns already told you to expect. That's a much smaller, much faster task than open-ended comprehension — you're verifying a specific hypothesis, not building one from scratch line by line.

This matters more for generated code than hand-written code, not less. A human author's variable names and comments often leak intent as you go; a fluent generated function can look equally confident regardless of whether the returns actually match what the name and signature promise — which is exactly the gap this order is built to catch fast.

contentSections.question: Before reading the body: given only `def reconcile_ledger(entries: list[dict], as_of: date) -> ReconciliationResult`, and that `ReconciliationResult` has fields `matched`, `unmatched`, `as_of` — what is this function most likely doing with `as_of`?
contentSections.hint: The parameter is threaded through to the output type unchanged. What would a reconciliation process need a cutoff date for?
contentSections.answer: It's almost certainly filtering `entries` to only those relevant as of that date — reconciliation is normally a snapshot operation, not an all-time one, and the fact that `as_of` reappears unchanged on the result (rather than being consumed into a computed value) suggests it's being carried through as a record of what cutoff was used, not just used internally and discarded. You can't confirm this without the body, but you now have something specific to check for, instead of reading the body cold.

contentSections.body: The signature and the return type are the fastest, densest source of intent in a function — read them before the body, and let the body answer a specific question instead of an open one.

contentSections.title: The body is a check, not a discovery

contentSections.body:
Once you've read the signature and every return, the body reading changes shape. You're not asking "what does this do?" from nothing — you're asking "does this actually get from the inputs to the outputs I was already told to expect?" That's a narrower, faster question, and it surfaces mismatches a top-to-bottom read tends to miss, because a top-to-bottom read has no expectation yet to check against.

This is especially sharp when a function has more than one `return`. Each early return is a distinct promise: a distinct condition under which the function concludes, and a distinct value it hands back for that condition. Reading all the returns before the body means you walk in already knowing how many endings to expect and roughly what should trigger each one — so when the body's logic doesn't cleanly map to one of them, that's the first thing worth flagging, not something you'd have caught by accident on your third re-read.

steps.label: Read the signature
steps.work: `computeShippingCost(order, destination)` — two inputs, no declared types (plain JS). Name promises a cost comes out.
steps.why: Even without types, the name and parameter names narrow the space: this is a pure calculation over an order and a destination, not something that mutates either.

steps.label: Read every return, before the body's logic
steps.work: Three returns: `{cost: null, reason: 'unserviceable'}`, `{cost: 0, reason: 'no_physical_items'}`, `{cost: <number>, reason: 'computed'}`. So the shape is always `{cost, reason}`, and there are exactly three distinct endings.
steps.why: This tells you the function was designed to explain itself via `reason`, not just return a bare number — and it tells you there are precisely three cases to hold the body accountable to, before you've read a line of the logic that produces them.

steps.label: Read the body as a check against those three cases
steps.work: Case 1 (unserviceable) is checked first and returns immediately — consistent. Case 2 (zero weight) is checked next — consistent. Case 3 sums weight × rate, adds a 40% priority surcharge, rounds to two decimals — the 'computed' case. All three returns are reachable and mutually exclusive.
steps.why: Because you already knew the three cases going in, verifying the body took one pass, checking each branch against an expectation, rather than building the whole mental model from scratch while also trying to spot problems.

blanks.prompt: From the signature alone, before reading further: what does this function most likely compute, and for whom?
blanks.answer: A late fee for an invoice, as of a given date — the return type name (FeeResult) and the two inputs (an invoice, today's date) are enough to guess this even before reading a return statement.
accept: a late payment fee for an invoice
how much fee an invoice owes
blanks.why: The signature alone narrows this to 'something about lateness and money,' which is most of the way to correct before any logic is read.

blanks.prompt: List the three distinct return cases, in the order they'd fire, based on reading only the return statements.
blanks.answer: 1) already paid → fee 0, waived. 2) not yet due (days_late <= 0) → fee 0, not waived. 3) late → a computed fee, capped.
blanks.why: Naming all three endings up front is what turns the body read into confirmation instead of discovery — you now know to look for exactly a cap and a per-day rate when you get to the third case.

blanks.prompt: Now read the body: does the 'late' case's fee calculation match what a per-day, capped fee should look like, or is something off?
blanks.answer: It matches: 1.5% of the balance per day late, capped at 25% of the balance total (via `min(...)`) — both a growth mechanism and a ceiling, which is what 'capped daily late fee' implies.
accept: matches — per-day rate with a cap
blanks.why: This is the payoff of the order: you're confirming a specific shape (rate × days, with a cap) rather than reverse-engineering the formula's intent from scratch.

contentSections.procedure: Signature narrows the space of what a function is for. Every return, read before the body, tells you how many distinct endings to expect and roughly what triggers each. The body read then becomes verification against a specific, small set of expectations — faster, and far more likely to catch a mismatch than a cold top-to-bottom read.

contentSections.body: Signature, then every return, then the body — in that order, the body read becomes a check against a specific hypothesis instead of a search with no starting point.

title: Naming as evidence — and as misdirection
description: A name is a claim about what code does, made by whoever wrote it — including a model that names things the same confident way whether the claim is true or not.

learningObjectives.text: Use function and variable names as a first hypothesis about intent, while treating them as unverified
Identify cases where a name overstates, understates, or misdescribes what the code beneath it actually does

contentSections.title: A name is a claim, not a fact

contentSections.body:
Names are genuinely useful evidence — a well-named function usually does roughly what it says, and reading names first is part of the signature-first technique from the last lesson. But a name is a *claim*, made by whoever wrote the code, and claims can be wrong without anyone lying: the author (human or model) believed the name was accurate, or named it aspirationally for what it was supposed to become, or copied a name from a similar-looking function that did more.

Generated code has a specific version of this risk. A model produces a plausible name and a plausible implementation from the same generation pass — nothing checks that the two actually agree with each other, the same way nothing checks that a docstring matches the logic beneath it. `sanitizeInput` is exactly the kind of name a model reaches for when asked to "handle user input safely," because it's a common, confident-sounding name for that class of task — regardless of whether the specific three lines underneath it actually constitute sanitization.

The practical habit: read the name as a hypothesis to check, not a fact to accept. For names that carry weight — anything implying validation, sanitization, authorization, or idempotency — go verify the body actually does what the name claims before you build anything else on top of the assumption that it does.

contentSections.question: The function is named `is_authorized` with a docstring confirming that name. What's actually wrong here?

options.label: It only checks that a user object exists (is logged in) — it never checks whether that specific user has permission for that specific resource
It should return None instead of a boolean when the user is missing
Nothing's wrong — `resource` being unused just means access is universal once logged in, which is a valid design

feedback.checks-login-not-permission: Correct. 'Authorized' means permitted to do this specific thing; this function only checks 'authenticated' — logged in at all. The parameter `resource` is accepted but never referenced in the body, which is the tell: a real authorization check would need to look at the resource to decide anything about it.
feedback.should-return-none: The return type isn't the problem here — a bool is a fine shape for an authorization check. The problem is what's being checked, not how the result is typed.
feedback.resource-unused-is-fine: An unused parameter in a function whose whole job is supposedly to reason about that parameter is a strong signal, not a neutral detail — 'universal access once logged in' is a real design some systems use, but nothing about the name `is_authorized` or the docstring suggests that's what's intended here; it reads as a gap, not a choice.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The name and docstring both assert a permission check against a specific resource. The body checks only `user is not None` — authentication, not authorization — and the unused `resource` parameter is the giveaway that the function was never wired up to actually reason about the resource at all. Code that calls this expecting real per-resource authorization will silently let any logged-in user through to anything, which is the exact shape of bug a name-trusting review misses and a body-reading review catches in one line.

contentSections.body: A name that implies a security or correctness property — authorized, sanitized, validated, safe — is a claim to verify against the body, not a fact to build on.

contentSections.title: Names that undersell, and names copied from elsewhere

contentSections.body:
Misdirection runs both ways. A name can overstate what code does (`sanitizeInput` that only trims) or understate it — a function called `formatDate` that also silently converts time zones is doing something a caller relying on the name alone won't expect. Both failure directions come from the same source: the name and the logic were written in the same pass, with nothing checking one against the other.

There's a third, specific pattern worth knowing: a name copied forward from a similar function nearby, where the logic was adapted but the name wasn't. This happens constantly when a model is shown one function as a pattern to follow and asked to write a related one — it often reuses naming conventions faithfully while the actual behavior diverges to fit the new case, and the result is a name that made perfect sense for the original and misleading sense for the copy.

contentSections.question: What does the name `formatDateForUser` fail to signal, given what the function actually does?

options.label: That it's applying a timezone shift before formatting, not just formatting — a caller reading only the name has no reason to expect the date to change, only how it's displayed
Nothing — the name accurately describes formatting a date for a user
That it takes a `user` object as a parameter

feedback.hides-shift: Right. 'Format' in the name promises a display transformation — same date, different string. The function actually shifts the date by the user's UTC offset before formatting, which can move the date itself across a day boundary near midnight. A caller who trusts the name and doesn't read the body could easily assume the underlying date value is untouched, which is exactly wrong.
feedback.name-fine: The name reads plausibly, which is the problem — it's plausible and incomplete. 'Formats a date for a user' undersells a real value change (the offset shift) as a cosmetic one (formatting), and that gap is invisible unless you read past the name.
feedback.hides-param: The parameter is visible right there in the signature — that's not hidden information. What's hidden is what the function *does* with that parameter, which the name doesn't disclose.

contentSections.concept: A name inherited from a similar-looking function nearby can be accurate for the original and misleading for the copy, because the logic diverged while the naming convention didn't. Copied structure is exactly where this risk concentrates — check whether a name that looked safe two functions ago still describes what the new function actually does.

contentSections.body: Misdirection isn't always overstatement — a name can undersell a real behavior change as cosmetic, especially when it was copied from a similar function whose logic has since diverged.

title: Comments that describe code that no longer exists
description: A comment is a snapshot of what someone believed the code did at the moment they wrote it — and the code beneath it keeps changing after the comment stops.

learningObjectives.text: Recognize when a comment describes an earlier version of the logic beneath it rather than the current one
Treat comments as a hypothesis to check against the code, not as a substitute for reading it

contentSections.title: The comment is a photograph

contentSections.body:
```python
# Retry up to 3 times with exponential backoff before giving up
def fetch_with_retry(url):
    response = requests.get(url, timeout=5)
    if response.status_code >= 500:
        response = requests.get(url, timeout=5)
    return response
```

The comment describes a retry loop with backoff. The code retries exactly once, with no backoff at all. Somewhere between whoever wrote that comment and the code as it stands now, the implementation changed and the comment didn't — or, in the AI-generated case, the comment and the code were never actually the same claim in the first place, just two plausible-sounding outputs from the same request.

A comment is not a live description of the code — it's a snapshot, true at some earlier moment, that nothing forces to stay true as the code around it changes. This is a known problem with hand-written code (comments rot faster than logic, because nothing errors when they diverge), and it has a distinct version with generated code: a model can produce a comment that describes the *intended* behavior from the prompt — three retries, exponential backoff — while the actual generated logic falls short of implementing all of it, because generating an accurate summary and generating fully correct logic are not the same task, done by the same process, with no check between them.

The practical rule: read the comment as a claim about what the code is supposed to do, then verify it against the actual logic the same way you'd verify a name. Where they disagree, the code is what runs — the comment is not documentation you can trust instead of reading, it's a hypothesis with the same standing as a function name.

contentSections.scenario: The `fetch_with_retry` function above: comment claims 3 retries with exponential backoff, code shows one retry with no backoff and the same 5-second timeout both times.
contentSections.question: What's the most accurate account of why the comment and the code disagree?

options.label: Someone edited the retry logic later and forgot to update the comment, the classic human-authored version of this problem

Comment and code both came from the same generation request — describing 'retry 3 times with exponential backoff' and fully implementing it are different tasks that don't automatically stay in sync just because one process produced both
There's no real disagreement — a single retry with the same timeout could be read as a minimal form of backoff

feedback.same-source-diff-fidelity: Right, for generated code specifically: the comment and the logic were produced together, in response to a request that probably did ask for retries with backoff. Writing an accurate-sounding summary of that request is easy; actually implementing a full retry loop with a backoff schedule is more work, and there's no internal check that forces the two to match. The comment reflects the request more faithfully than the code does.
feedback.code-was-edited: This is the classic explanation for hand-written code, and it can't be ruled out in general — but nothing in this snippet shows evidence of a later edit (no removed lines, no version history shown), and the far more common cause in freshly generated code is the mismatch between summarizing intent and fully implementing it in one pass.
feedback.backoff-implied: A single retry with an identical timeout isn't a minimal form of exponential backoff — backoff specifically means increasing delay between attempts, and there's no delay of any kind here, let alone an increasing one. This reads the comment into the code rather than checking the code against the comment.

contentSections.mechanism: Comments and logic can diverge in hand-written code through edits that miss the comment. In generated code there's an additional, more direct route: the comment can be a faithful echo of what was asked for, while the logic is a partial or approximate implementation of that same ask — two outputs of one generation pass, with nothing enforcing that they describe the same behavior. Either way, the fix is the same: read the comment as a claim, then check it against what the code actually does, not the other way around.

contentSections.body: A comment is a claim made at some point about the code — possibly never fully true, possibly true once and no longer. Check it against the logic; don't read it as the logic.

contentSections.title: When the comment is the only spec you have

contentSections.body:
None of this means comments are useless — a comment that turns out to be wrong is still telling you something real: what someone (or some prompt) believed the requirement was. That's often the closest thing to a written spec you'll get for undocumented code, and a comment that contradicts its own code is a strong, specific signal of exactly where to look first — better than a comment that agrees with the code, which tells you nothing you couldn't get from reading the code alone.

So the useful move isn't to distrust comments generally, it's to treat a mismatch as a lead: the comment is evidence of an intended requirement the code doesn't fully meet, which is often more actionable than either the comment or the code would be alone. "Retry 3 times with exponential backoff" plus code that retries once is a much clearer bug report than either "this comment might be stale" or "this code seems incomplete" would be on their own.

contentSections.scenario: Five comment/code pairs from a generated codebase you're reviewing.
contentSections.question: Select every pair where the comment is worth treating as a lead pointing at a real gap in the code beneath it.

items.label: `# Cache results for 5 minutes` above code with no expiry logic at all — results are cached forever once set
`# Returns the user's full name, or None if not set` above code that does exactly that, nothing more
`# Sort orders newest first` above `orders.sort(key=lambda o: o.created_at)` with no `reverse=True`
`# Efficiently processes the batch` above a straightforward for-loop with no particular optimization
`# Idempotent — safe to call multiple times` above code that increments a counter with no guard against duplicate calls

explanation.cache-ttl: A real, checkable gap: the comment names a specific expiry duration, the code implements no expiry mechanism at all. This is a concrete lead — go check what happens to memory or staleness over time.
explanation.matches-code: No gap here — the comment and code agree, which means the comment isn't giving you information beyond what the code already shows. Not a lead, just confirmation.
explanation.sort-desc: A real gap: 'newest first' requires descending order, and a default `.sort()` on `created_at` produces ascending (oldest first) order. The missing `reverse=True` is exactly the kind of specific, checkable mismatch a comment-as-lead surfaces.
explanation.vague-praise: "Efficiently" isn't a checkable claim — there's no specific behavior to verify it against, so it's not a lead pointing anywhere in particular, just filler.
explanation.idempotent-claim: A real and serious gap: 'idempotent' has a specific technical meaning — calling it twice should produce the same result as calling it once — and an unguarded increment is the textbook counterexample. This is the highest-value kind of lead, because the claim is both specific and safety-relevant.

contentSections.synthesis: The comments worth chasing make a specific, checkable claim that the code visibly doesn't meet — a duration, an order, a guarantee like idempotency. Vague comments and comments that just restate the code aren't leads either way; they're not lying, but they're also not telling you anything the code doesn't already say.

contentSections.body: A comment that contradicts its code is a lead, not noise — it's often the closest thing you have to a written requirement, pointing exactly at the gap between what was intended and what shipped.

title: Reconstructing the requirement from the implementation
description: When there's no ticket, no comment, and no one to ask, the specific numbers and branches in the code are themselves evidence of what the requirement was.

learningObjectives.text: Infer an unstated business rule from specific constants, thresholds, and branch conditions in code
Distinguish an inference well-supported by the code's specifics from a guess dressed up as one

contentSections.title: Specific numbers are never accidents

contentSections.body:
When there's no written spec, the implementation is frequently the only record of what was actually decided — and it's a more reliable record than it looks, because specific constants and specific branch conditions are expensive to get by accident. Nobody types `0.015` instead of a round number like `0.01` or `0.02` unless that number came from somewhere: a contract term, a regulatory cap, a decision made in a meeting and never written down anywhere except in this one function.

The technique: when you hit code with no documented rationale, look specifically at what varies and what's fixed. A fixed cap (`min(fee, balance * 0.25)`) is a strong signal of an intentional ceiling — someone decided fees shouldn't exceed a quarter of the balance, for a reason that probably has nothing to do with this specific function and everything to do with a policy this function is one implementation of. A specific rate (`0.015`) that isn't a clean round number is a signal it was copied from an authoritative source — a contract, a rate table — rather than picked by whoever wrote this code.

This isn't guessing. It's treating the implementation as evidence and reasoning from what's specific and deliberate-looking to what requirement would produce exactly that shape — the same kind of inference a detective makes from a specific detail at a scene, not a shrug that says 'could be anything.'

contentSections.question: Before being told anything else about this business: what's your best guess for the actual, real-world policy reason a cap of exactly 30% would exist, rather than 25% or 50%?
contentSections.unit: % (your reasoning, not a literal further number)
contentSections.explanation: There's no single right story — the exercise is in noticing that 30% specifically, not 'a cap' generically, is what needs explaining. Plausible real reasons: a margin floor (the business can't discount past the point where a sale stops being profitable, and 30% is where that floor sits for this product line), a coupon-stacking policy (individual promotions cap lower, but this is the ceiling across all combined promotions), or a legal/contractual maximum from a supplier agreement. What matters is the habit: a specific number like 30% is evidence of one of these being true, and it's worth writing '30% cap — reason unknown, check with product/finance' into your review notes rather than treating the number as incidental.

contentSections.body: A specific constant or a fixed cap in code with no comment isn't arbitrary — it's evidence of a decision made somewhere else, and worth naming as an open question rather than passing over.

contentSections.title: Branches encode conditions someone thought mattered

contentSections.body:
The same logic applies to branch conditions, not just numeric constants. An `if` statement checking a specific, oddly precise condition is evidence that someone (or some prompt) thought that exact condition mattered enough to special-case — and reconstructing *why* it mattered is often more useful for review than just confirming the branch works.

The risk on the other side: over-reading. Not every specific number or branch is meaningful — sometimes a threshold really is arbitrary, or copied from an unrelated example the model was shown. The discipline is to distinguish inference that's well-supported by the code's own specifics from a story you're telling because a story feels more satisfying than 'I don't know.' A well-supported inference points at *what to go verify* — ask someone, check a contract, look for the number elsewhere in the codebase — rather than stopping at a plausible-sounding guess and treating it as settled.

contentSections.title: The unexplained branch

start.situation: You need to decide how to handle this in review, since nobody can immediately explain the $500 and country-mismatch condition.
start.question: What's your first move?

choices.label: Approve it — the logic runs without error and the numbers are plausible enough for fraud-adjacent review triggers
choices.consequence: Three weeks later, someone asks why orders exactly at $500 shipping domestically never get flagged, and nobody can explain the $500 figure or the international-shipping specifically. It ships anyway because nobody owns the question.

choices.label: Write a comment guessing it's a fraud-risk heuristic (mismatched billing/shipping country plus a high order value is a classic fraud signal) and move on
choices.consequence: The guess is directionally reasonable — but you never actually confirmed whether $500 is this company's real threshold or a number the model reached for as a plausible-sounding default.

choices.label: Flag both thresholds explicitly in the review: 'these look like fraud/logistics review triggers based on the shape of the conditions — need to confirm the actual $500 and 20-item thresholds against whatever policy this implements before merging'
choices.consequence: The reviewer chases it down before merge, not after.

confirm.situation: Whoever wrote the ticket (found via a linked Slack thread) confirms: $500 + country mismatch is indeed a fraud heuristic pulled from the payment processor's own risk guidance, and 20+ items is a warehouse capacity trigger, unrelated to fraud at all — packages that large need a different fulfillment path.
confirm.question: Given that the two branches turned out to encode two completely unrelated policies bundled into one function, what's the useful next step?

choices.label: Leave it as one function — it works, and splitting it is just refactoring for its own sake
choices.consequence: Six months later, someone touches the fraud threshold to update it for a policy change and doesn't realize they're now also affecting when large orders get flagged for warehouse routing — an unrelated system breaks.

choices.label: Split into two functions — `is_fraud_risk` and `needs_warehouse_review` — each with the confirmed policy source cited, even though the two happened to be combined in the original
choices.consequence: The two concerns are now independently changeable, and the next person who touches either one has the actual policy source right there instead of having to reconstruct it again.

unverified.summary: An unexplained, specific threshold shipped unverified, and the review that could have caught it happened after the fact instead of before.
unverified.lesson: Plausible-looking numbers aren't the same as confirmed ones. 'Runs without error' answers a different question than 'is this the right threshold' — and only the second one is what review is actually for.

coupled.summary: The immediate review question got answered, but two unrelated policies stayed silently coupled in one function, and that coupling caused a real incident later.
coupled.lesson: Reconstructing *why* a branch exists is only half the job when the reconstruction reveals two unrelated concerns bundled together — the fix isn't just understanding the code, it's separating what shouldn't have been combined.

resolved.summary: Both thresholds got a confirmed source, and the accidental coupling between two unrelated policies got separated before it could cause a cross-system bug.
resolved.lesson: Reconstructing intent from specific numbers is the first step. Verifying the reconstruction with whoever actually owns the policy, and then acting on what that verification reveals — including untangling accidental coupling — is what turns a good guess into a real fix.

contentSections.body: A well-supported inference from specific code tells you what to go verify, not what to assume. Treat a plausible reconstruction as a question to confirm, not a conclusion to build on.

title: Saying what a function does in one sentence
description: If you can't compress a function into one accurate sentence, you haven't actually finished reading it — and the compression itself is what exposes what you're still unsure about.

learningObjectives.text: Compress a function's behavior into a single accurate sentence covering its normal case and its stated exceptions
Use the difficulty of writing that sentence as a signal that a function is doing more than one thing

contentSections.title: One sentence is a compression test

contentSections.body:
Four lessons in this module have been about gathering evidence — signatures, names, comments, unstated requirements. This one is about the payoff: can you say, in one sentence, what a function actually does? Not what it's named, not what its comment claims — what the code, as read, actually does.

"Computes the median of a sorted list, correctly averaging the two middle values for even-length lists, and returns `None` for an empty list" is one sentence and it's precise: normal case, the tricky case (even-length), and the edge case (empty), all named. "Handles the median calculation" is also one sentence, and it says almost nothing — it would be equally true of a function with three known bugs.

The one-sentence test isn't a communication exercise tacked on after the real work of reading — it's a check on whether the reading actually happened. A sentence that's accurate and specific requires you to have actually traced the returns, noticed the edge cases, and understood how the branches relate to each other — everything the last four lessons practiced. A sentence that's vague ("handles X," "processes the data," "does the calculation") is often a sign the reading stopped short, whether or not the reader realizes it.

The useful discipline: force the sentence to name the normal case *and* at least one exception or edge case the function specifically handles differently. If you can't find an exception to name, either the function genuinely has none (worth noting — is that actually complete?) or you haven't looked closely enough yet to find the one it does have.

fields.prompt: What's the core action, in a few words?
options: Computes the next billing date for a subscription
fields.correctValue: Computes the next billing date for a subscription
fields.feedback: Right — that's what the function returns in its main cases, and the name confirms it.

fields.prompt: What does it do differently for different plan types?
options: Adds exactly one calendar year for annual plans, and 30 days for everything else
Always adds exactly 30 days regardless of plan
Asks the payment processor for the next date
fields.correctValue: Adds exactly one calendar year for annual plans, and 30 days for everything else
fields.feedback: Right — and note the distinction worth keeping in the sentence: a calendar year (which can land on a different day count depending on leap years) versus a fixed 30-day offset for non-annual plans, which isn't quite 'monthly' for every calendar month.

fields.prompt: What's the one case where it doesn't compute a date at all?
options: When the subscription is cancelled, it returns None instead
When the subscription is annual, it returns None
fields.correctValue: When the subscription is cancelled, it returns None instead
fields.feedback: Right — this is the exception the one-sentence description has to name, or it's silently claiming the function always returns a date, which it doesn't.

contentSections.synthesis: Assembled: 'Computes a subscription's next billing date as one calendar year after its start date for annual plans or 30 days after for everything else, returning None instead if the subscription has been cancelled.' That's one sentence, and it names the normal case, the branch that changes behavior (annual vs. everything else), and the exception (cancelled → None) — which is exactly the shape a compression that actually required reading the whole function produces.

contentSections.body: A one-sentence description that names the normal case and at least one real exception is evidence you actually read the function. A vague sentence usually means the reading stopped early.

contentSections.title: When one sentence won't fit

contentSections.body:
Sometimes the honest one-sentence attempt keeps growing a third and fourth clause, and no version of it feels like it's actually one coherent idea. That difficulty is itself useful information — not a failure of your compression skills, but a signal that the function is doing more than one job, stitched together because it was convenient to write it that way, not because the two jobs belong together.

A function that genuinely does one thing compresses cleanly, almost always, once you've actually traced its branches. A function that resists compression — where every attempt at one sentence needs an 'and also' that isn't really related to the first clause — is a function whose responsibilities should probably be two functions. This is the same signal the case-sim in the previous lesson surfaced (the fraud-check-and-warehouse-routing function bundled into one) from a different angle: reading for intent doesn't just tell you what code does, it tells you when what it does shouldn't be one thing.

contentSections.question: A function called `processOrder` has a one-sentence description that reads: 'Validates the order's payment method, charges the customer, updates inventory counts, sends a confirmation email, and logs the transaction for analytics.' Is that a sign of a well-compressed sentence, or a sign of something else?
contentSections.hint: Count the number of genuinely distinct responsibilities in that sentence, connected by 'and.'
contentSections.answer: It's a sign the function is doing five distinct jobs (validation, payment, inventory, notification, analytics) that happen to be sequenced together, not one job describable in one real sentence — the 'and, and, and' structure is the tell. A one-sentence description should read as one idea with at most one qualifying exception, the way the billing-date example did. When it reads as a list stitched together with conjunctions, that's usually evidence the function should be split — each responsibility independently readable, testable, and reviewable — rather than evidence you just need a longer sentence.

contentSections.body: If your one-sentence attempt keeps needing another 'and' for an unrelated responsibility, that's not a compression failure — it's the function telling you it's actually several functions.

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Every lesson this module used a single function at a time. Real undocumented code rarely comes in single functions — it comes in modules, where the functions reference each other, and the module's actual purpose only becomes clear once you've read several of them together. This lab is that: one real module, reverse-engineered into a spec, with every assumption you couldn't verify named as exactly that.

contentSections.title: Reverse-engineer a module's spec
contentSections.brief: Pick a real module from a codebase you have access to (your own project, an open-source repo, work code) that has little or no documentation — no README section, no doc comments beyond the occasional stray note, nobody left to ask. Check every name, comment, and specific constant against what the logic actually does — note every mismatch you find, the way the lesson's examples did. rubric.criterion: Every public function has a genuinely one-sentence, specific description
rubric.meets: The sentence names the normal case and at least one exception or edge case, not a vague restatement of the function's name.

rubric.meets: If the module has zero mismatches, the spec says so explicitly rather than silently omitting the check — 'no name or comment mismatches found' is a real finding, not nothing.

rubric.criterion: The module's overall purpose paragraph is consistent with all the individual function sentences
rubric.meets: Nothing in the per-function descriptions contradicts the module-level summary — if it does, that's worth resolving before submitting, not leaving as a loose thread.

contentSections.body: A spec reconstructed from real code and honestly marked for what's confirmed versus inferred is a genuinely useful artefact — often more useful than an outdated written spec would have been.

title: Tracing a happy path by hand
description: Before you can find the case a function got wrong, you need to be able to walk one case through it correctly — with real values, not a vibe.

learningObjectives.text: Trace a function's happy path step by step with concrete example values, tracking every variable's value as it changes
Distinguish an actual hand trace from a plausible-sounding summary of what the code probably does

contentSections.title: One concrete input, all the way through

contentSections.body:
A generated function for splitting a restaurant bill:

```python
def split_bill(total, people, tip_pct):
    tip = total * (tip_pct / 100)
    grand_total = total + tip
    per_person = grand_total / len(people)
    return {p: round(per_person, 2) for p in people}
```

"Looks right" is not the same claim as "I traced it." Pick real numbers — `total=100`, `people=['A', 'B', 'C']`, `tip_pct=20` — and walk them through: `tip = 100 * 0.2 = 20`. `grand_total = 120`. `per_person = 120 / 3 = 40.0`. Result: `{'A': 40.0, 'B': 40.0, 'C': 40.0}`. That took fifteen seconds and it's the difference between believing the function is right and knowing one specific case of it is.

Tracing by hand means picking concrete values, then updating every variable's actual value line by line as the code executes — not summarizing what a section "does" in prose, which is where skimming quietly substitutes for tracing. The test of whether you actually traced something: could you write down the value of every variable at the point the function returns, without re-reading the code to check?

This matters more before you go looking for bugs, not after. Reviewers who jump straight to "what could go wrong" without first confirming the normal case actually works end up debating hypothetical edge cases against a mental model of the function that was never verified to be correct even for the input it was obviously built for. One traced happy path anchors everything else you check against it.

Generated code raises the stakes slightly: a function can look identical in structure to a hundred correct examples the model was trained on and still have one arithmetic detail wrong — a wrong divisor, an operator flipped — that only shows up once you actually compute the numbers rather than pattern-match the shape of the code.

contentSections.problem:
Trace this generated discount function by hand for a concrete cart.

```python
def price_cart(items, member_discount_pct):
    subtotal = sum(item['price'] * item['qty'] for item in items)
    discount = subtotal * (member_discount_pct / 100)
    return round(subtotal - discount, 2)
```

Input: `items = [{'price': 12.50, 'qty': 2}, {'price': 5.00, 'qty': 1}]`, `member_discount_pct = 10`.

steps.label: Compute subtotal
steps.why: Tracing the generator expression term by term is the only way to be sure `qty` is actually being multiplied in, not just added.

steps.label: Compute discount
steps.why: This is where a wrong divisor would show up — if the code had said `member_discount_pct / 1000` by mistake, this step is exactly where you'd catch it, and only because you're using real numbers instead of eyeballing the expression.

steps.label: Compute and round the result
steps.why: The final value is now a fact you derived, not an impression you formed — you could defend `27.0` to someone else with the arithmetic, not just the shape of the code.

faded.problem:
Trace this generated shipping-tier function for a concrete order.

```python
def shipping_tier(order_total, is_member):
    threshold = 35 if is_member else 50
    if order_total >= threshold:
        return 'free'
    return 'standard'
```

Input: `order_total = 40`, `is_member = True`.

blanks.prompt: What value does `threshold` take, and why?
blanks.answer: 35, because `is_member` is `True`, taking the first branch of the conditional expression.
blanks.why: Conditional expressions (`x if cond else y`) still need to be traced with the actual truth value, not assumed from reading the shape of the line.

blanks.prompt: Does `order_total >= threshold` evaluate to True or False here, with the real numbers?
blanks.why: This is the step a skim skips: confirming the comparison with the actual numbers rather than the general sense that '40 seems like it should qualify.'

blanks.prompt: What does the function return for this input?
blanks.why: A traced happy path ends in a specific, defensible value — not 'probably free' but 'free, because 40 >= 35 with threshold correctly resolved to the member rate.'

contentSections.procedure: Pick concrete values for every input. Update every variable's actual value at each line, including inside comprehensions and conditional expressions. Arrive at a specific final value you derived, not one you're pattern-matching from having seen similar code before.

contentSections.body: A happy-path trace ends in a specific value you can defend with arithmetic, not a summary you're pattern-matching from code that looks familiar.

contentSections.title: Why the happy path comes first

contentSections.body:
It's tempting to skip straight to hunting for the broken case, especially once you already suspect a function has a bug — that instinct is usually right to have, but wrong to act on first. If you haven't confirmed the ordinary case with real numbers, you don't actually have a baseline to compare the suspicious case against, and it becomes easy to misdiagnose a real bug as expected behavior, or invent a bug that isn't there because your mental model of the 'correct' output was never checked either.

The happy-path trace is also what makes the rest of this module's techniques fast rather than slow. Once you know exactly how one concrete input flows through the function — which branch it takes, which variables it touches — every other case you check is a diff against that baseline: same input with one thing changed, tracing only what's different. That's a much smaller task than re-deriving the whole function from scratch for every case you check.

contentSections.question: A reviewer skips tracing the happy path and jumps straight to checking what happens with an empty `items` list in `price_cart`. They report: "looks fine, `sum()` of an empty list is `0`, so subtotal is `0`, discount is `0`, result is `0`." What did skipping the happy-path trace cost them here?
contentSections.hint: The edge-case trace they did is arithmetically correct. What haven't they established about the function that the empty-list case alone can't tell them?
contentSections.answer: The edge case they checked is correct, but they still don't know whether the *normal*, non-empty case computes the right number — the case that will run on almost every real order. A reviewer who never traced a normal cart with real prices and quantities has approved the function's most common path purely on the strength of the code's shape looking plausible, which is exactly the gap a happy-path trace closes and an edge-case-only check doesn't.

contentSections.body: Trace the ordinary case first, with real numbers, before hunting for the broken one — it gives you a verified baseline instead of an assumed one.

title: Every branch is a promise about a case that exists
description: An if/elif/else chain is a claim about how many distinct situations the author believed could occur. Reading the branches tells you what they believed — and whether they were right.

learningObjectives.text: Enumerate the distinct cases a branching structure claims to handle, and check that claim against what can actually occur
Identify a branch condition inherited from a similar pattern that doesn't actually apply to the real domain of values

contentSections.title: Count the branches, name the case each one claims

contentSections.body:
Every branch in a conditional chain is a claim that a specific case exists and needs to be handled differently from the others. Reading a branch structure for intent means reading it as a list of claims, not just a list of code paths: "this author believed there are exactly these N distinct situations." The `else` or final `elif` is the least examined branch in most reviews and often the most important, because it's a catch-all claim about everything not explicitly named — and catch-all claims are exactly where an incomplete understanding of the real domain hides.

This is a specific risk with generated branches: a model producing an `if/elif/else` chain is often pattern-completing from similar branching structures it's seen, which reliably produces syntactically clean chains that don't always reflect the actual, current shape of your domain's data. A three-way country split that's correct for a business that ships in North America only can be quietly wrong the day that business starts shipping to the EU, and nothing about the code itself signals that the branch structure hasn't been re-examined against the new reality.

The habit: for every branch, name the specific case it claims to handle, out loud or in writing. For the `else`, name what it's implicitly claiming is true about everything not named above it. If you can't confidently say that claim is still accurate, that's the branch to go verify first, not the one to skim past because it's the shortest line in the function.

contentSections.question: What does the `else` branch's claim get wrong here, and what's the concrete consequence?

options.label: It silently claims `enterprise_plus` customers — the highest tier — belong in the same bucket as `free` customers, giving the company's biggest accounts 'normal' priority instead of at least 'urgent'
Nothing is wrong — `else` correctly catches every tier not explicitly named, which is exactly what a catch-all should do
The bug is that `free` tier isn't given its own explicit branch

feedback.enterprise-plus-miscategorized: Exactly this. The `else` branch's implicit claim — 'everything not enterprise or pro is normal priority' — was true when the function was written against a three-tier world, and became false the moment a fourth, higher tier was added, without a single line of this function changing. `enterprise_plus` customers, the company's most valuable accounts, now get the same 'normal' priority as customers on the free tier, and nothing about running the code raises an error to reveal it.
feedback.else-is-fine: A catch-all branch correctly catching everything unnamed isn't the problem — whether its *implicit claim about what those unnamed cases deserve* is still accurate is the problem. Here it isn't: it lumps the highest tier in with the lowest under a claim that made sense for an older, smaller set of tiers.
feedback.free-tier-missing: `free` tier customers are in fact correctly handled by the `else` branch — the miscategorization isn't about `free`, it's about a newer tier the branch structure was never updated to know exists at all.

contentSections.concept: A branch chain's `else` is an implicit claim about everything not named above it, and that claim can go stale the moment the domain grows a new case — silently, with no error, because the code still runs without complaint against the new value.

contentSections.body: Name the case each branch claims to handle, including what the final `else` implicitly claims about everything else — that catch-all claim is where an outdated understanding of the domain hides longest.

contentSections.title: A branch that can never fire is also a claim worth checking

contentSections.body:
The opposite failure is just as common and just as easy to miss: a branch condition that looks meaningful but can structurally never be reached, because an earlier branch already claims every case it would have handled. This isn't a cosmetic issue — dead branches are frequently the sign of a requirement the author had in mind but implemented in the wrong place, meaning the actual requirement isn't met anywhere in the function even though it visibly appears to be handled.

Spotting this requires reading branches in relation to each other, not one at a time: does an earlier condition's range of matched values already fully cover a later condition's range? If so, the later branch's claim is never tested against real input, no matter how sensible it looks sitting there in the code.

contentSections.question: The second branch is meant to handle a specific case. What's actually wrong?

options.label: The `expedited_only` branch can never execute — any order with `days_since_purchase <= 14` already satisfies `<= 30` and returns 'eligible' first, so the second condition is dead code
The comparisons should use `<` instead of `<=`
The function needs a check for negative `days_since_purchase` values

feedback.unreachable-branch: Right. The branches are checked in order, and `<= 30` is a strictly wider condition than `<= 14` — every value that would satisfy the second condition already satisfied the first one and returned. Whatever business rule the author intended for orders 0-14 days old (an 'expedited' refund path, presumably faster or different from the general 30-day window) is never actually applied by this code, despite the branch sitting right there looking like it handles it.
feedback.wrong-comparison-operator: Switching `<=` to `<` doesn't fix the ordering problem — the second branch would still be a subset of the first regardless of whether the boundary is inclusive or exclusive, because 30 is still a wider window than 14.
feedback.missing-negative-check: A negative `days_since_purchase` is a real, separate concern worth flagging in its own right, but it's not what's wrong with the specific branch this question is about, and it doesn't explain why the `expedited_only` case never fires for any input.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The branches needed to be ordered narrowest-condition-first for this pattern to work: check `<= 14` before `<= 30`, so the tighter case gets a chance to match before the wider one swallows it. As written, the intended three-tier structure (0-14 days: expedited, 15-30 days: eligible, 31+: expired) collapses into an effective two-tier structure (0-30: eligible, 31+: expired) with a completely dead branch in the middle — a real gap in the refund policy that looks, on a casual read, like it's already covered.

contentSections.body: A branch that looks like it handles a case can still be structurally unreachable if an earlier, wider condition already claims every value it would have matched — check branch order, not just branch content.

title: Early returns, guard clauses, and the paths they hide
description: A guard clause that quietly returns a default value handles the case without ever telling anyone it happened — which is fine for some cases and a hidden failure for others.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish a guard clause that correctly short-circuits a real edge case from one that silently absorbs an input the caller needed to know about
Trace what a function's caller actually receives when a guard clause fires, not just whether the function itself avoids crashing

contentSections.title: A guard clause is a decision about what the caller finds out

contentSections.body:
Guard clauses are a genuinely good pattern — checking a precondition and returning early keeps a function's main logic flat and readable instead of nested three levels deep inside `if` blocks. The risk isn't the pattern, it's what happens to the information at the moment a guard clause fires: does the caller still get to know *which* precondition failed, or does everything collapse into one generic signal that erases the distinction?

This matters most when the different failure cases actually call for different behavior downstream. A checkout page that gets `None` back from `get_active_subscription` can't tell the difference between 'show a sign-up prompt' (no user, or never subscribed) and 'show a reactivate-your-subscription prompt' (had one, it lapsed) — the guard clauses threw that distinction away on the way out, even though the function's own logic clearly knew which case it was in at the moment each guard fired.

The habit: for every early return in a guard clause, ask what the caller actually receives, and whether that's enough information for the caller to do the right thing next. A guard clause that returns the same generic value for meaningfully different situations is a place where real information is being discarded inside the function, invisibly to anyone just reading the call site.

contentSections.question: Given the code, what's the actual root cause of the vague user complaint?

options.label: All three distinct failure reasons — empty cart, an out-of-stock item, a missing address — collapse into the same `false`, so the UI built on top of this function has no way to tell the user which one applies
The boolean logic itself is incorrect and sometimes returns `false` for carts that should be checkoutable
The function needs to show a loading spinner while checking stock

feedback.collapsed-boolean: Right. The function's internal logic is fine at distinguishing the three cases — each guard clause fires on a specific, distinct condition — but the moment each one returns bare `false`, that distinction is gone. Whatever UI calls `canCheckout(cart)` can only ever know 'not checkoutable,' never 'because of what.' The fix isn't the logic, it's the return shape: something like a reason code or a result object that preserves which guard fired.
feedback.logic-is-wrong: Nothing in the given code suggests the three conditions are evaluated incorrectly — each one does correctly detect its specific case. The bug isn't in *whether* it's false, it's in the total loss of information about *why* once it is.
feedback.needs-loading-state: A loading state addresses a different problem (asynchronous stock checks) that isn't described anywhere in this scenario — the bug report is specifically about users not knowing *why* the button is disabled, which points at the collapsed return value, not at timing.

contentSections.mechanism: Each guard clause correctly detects its own specific precondition failure, but returning the same generic `false` (or `None`, or any single default) for all of them destroys the distinction the moment execution leaves the function. The caller inherits a strictly poorer signal than the function itself actually had internally at the point each guard fired — and that loss is invisible unless you specifically trace what value survives to the return.

contentSections.body: A guard clause knows exactly which precondition failed at the moment it fires — check whether that knowledge survives into what the caller actually receives, or gets flattened into one generic signal.

contentSections.title: When a default is a case being silently accepted, not rejected

contentSections.body:
There's a second guard-clause risk, the mirror image of the first: a guard clause that returns a plausible-looking default value instead of surfacing that something unexpected happened at all. `if not price: return 0` looks like defensive programming — it prevents a crash on missing data — but from the caller's side, a `0` that means 'this item is free' and a `0` that means 'the price was missing and we made one up' are indistinguishable, and only one of those is actually true.

The question to ask of every guard clause that returns a default rather than raising or signaling an error: is this default a legitimate value for the normal case, or is it standing in for 'something's wrong and I didn't want to crash'? The first is a real design choice. The second is a bug quietly wearing the guard-clause pattern as camouflage, and it's specifically dangerous because the code runs without complaint — there's no stack trace pointing at it, no test failure, just a wrong number flowing silently downstream.

contentSections.scenario: Four guard clauses from a generated inventory system.
contentSections.question: Select every one where the default returned is standing in for a real error, rather than a legitimate normal-case value.

items.label: `if item.price is None: return 0` — treats a missing price the same as a genuinely free item
`if not cart.items: return 0` for a function computing cart total — an empty cart legitimately costs $0
`if item.quantity is None: return 1` — silently assumes a quantity of exactly one whenever the field wasn't set, with no signal that it was assumed rather than specified
`if not user.is_authenticated: return []` for a function listing a user's saved items — a logged-out user genuinely has no saved items to show

explanation.missing-price-zero: A missing price and an intentionally free item are different facts about the world, and this guard clause makes them indistinguishable — `0` downstream could mean either, and anything doing math on prices (revenue reports, discount calculations) would silently treat missing data as a real $0 sale.
explanation.empty-cart-zero-total: This one's legitimate: an empty cart really does cost nothing, and `0` is the mathematically correct total, not a stand-in for missing information — there's no ambiguity about what `0` means here.
explanation.missing-quantity-one: Same shape as the missing-price case: `1` is a plausible-looking normal value, but it's standing in for 'this field wasn't set,' and a caller has no way to tell 'quantity is genuinely 1' from 'quantity was never recorded and we guessed.'
explanation.unauthenticated-empty-list: Also legitimate — a logged-out user has no saved items in any meaningful sense, so an empty list isn't hiding a missing fact, it's accurately describing the actual state.

contentSections.synthesis: The distinguishing question is whether the returned value would still be true if you had complete information, or whether it's filling a gap where information is actually missing. `0` for an empty cart is true either way; `0` for a missing price is only true if the price actually is zero, which the guard clause has no way of confirming and no way of telling anyone it didn't confirm.

contentSections.body: A default value returned by a guard clause is only safe when it would be true regardless of missing information — otherwise it's an error wearing the shape of a normal case, silently, with nothing downstream able to tell the difference.

title: Mutable state and who else can change it
description: A function that reads or writes shared state is only as understandable as the answer to one question: what else, anywhere in the system, can also touch that same state?

learningObjectives.text: Identify shared mutable state a function depends on or modifies, distinct from its own local variables
Trace a concrete scenario where two callers touching the same mutable state produce a wrong result neither caller's code alone would suggest

contentSections.title: Local variables are safe. Shared state is a question about everyone else

contentSections.body:
A function's own local variables are safe to reason about in isolation — nothing outside the function can see or touch them while it runs. Shared mutable state is a completely different category: a module-level variable, a class attribute, an object passed by reference and mutated in place, a row in a database read and written without a lock. Understanding a function that touches shared state requires answering a question the function's own code never fully answers on its own: who else can read or write this same state, and when, relative to this function's own reads and writes?

This is exactly the kind of correctness bug that a happy-path trace, done by one caller calling the function once, cannot catch — tracing `check_rate_limit(user_id=42)` in isolation produces a perfectly correct-looking result every time, because the bug only exists in the gap *between* two overlapping calls, a scenario a single trace structurally can't represent. Finding this class of bug means specifically asking: could this function be called again, by something else, before this call finishes updating the state it depends on?

For generated code, this risk is easy to underweight, because a function like `check_rate_limit` reads as clean, idiomatic, textbook rate-limiting logic — the kind of code that appears correct in isolation in thousands of tutorials that never show it under concurrent load. Fluency in the single-caller case says nothing about safety in the multiple-caller case.

contentSections.question: Two nearly-simultaneous requests for the same `user_id`, both starting when `count` is already 9. Put the four operations in an interleaved order that results in BOTH requests being approved — a violation of the intended 10-request limit.
steps: Request B reads `_rate_limit_cache.get(user_id, 0)` → also gets 9, before A has written anything back
Request A writes `_rate_limit_cache[user_id] = 10` and returns True (approved)
Request B writes `_rate_limit_cache[user_id] = 10` and returns True (approved)
contentSections.explanation: Both requests read the same stale value (9) before either one's write is visible to the other — that's the entire mechanism of the bug. Neither request's own code is wrong in isolation; each one correctly reads, compares, and increments. The bug lives entirely in the gap between two callers' reads and writes overlapping in time, which is exactly why a single-caller trace can never surface it: there's no interleaving to trace when only one caller exists. This is the concrete shape of 'who else can touch this state' — the answer here is 'another request for the same user, arriving close enough in time,' and that answer only becomes visible once you deliberately consider more than one caller at once.

contentSections.body: A function's own logic can be correct in isolation and still be wrong under shared state — the bug lives in the gap between two callers' reads and writes, which a single trace structurally cannot show you.

contentSections.title: Mutation you didn't mean to share

contentSections.body:
A second, quieter version of the same risk: a function that mutates an object it was merely handed, rather than one it owns, without anyone at the call site expecting that. In languages where objects, lists, and dicts are passed by reference, a function that looks purely computational — takes an input, returns an output — can still leave the caller's original data changed underneath them, because 'in' and 'mutated' aren't mutually exclusive.

A specific, well-known trap in this family: a mutable default argument. `def add_tag(item, tags=[])` looks like it gives every call a fresh empty list to work with — it doesn't. The default list is created exactly once, when the function is defined, and every call that doesn't pass its own `tags` argument shares and mutates that same one list, across every caller, for the lifetime of the program. This reads as ordinary, idiomatic-looking code, and it's one of the most consistently reported real bugs in generated Python for exactly that reason: it's syntactically unremarkable and semantically wrong.

contentSections.question: Called twice, once as `add_tag('urgent')` and once as `add_tag('billing')`, with no `tags` argument passed either time — what's actually wrong?

options.label: The default list `tags=[]` is created once, at function definition time, and shared across every call that omits the argument — the second call returns `['urgent', 'billing']`, not a fresh `['billing']`, because both calls mutated the same underlying list
The bug is that the function sometimes returns a list and sometimes returns nothing
`list.append` is inefficient and should be replaced with a different data structure

feedback.shared-default-mutated: Right. Python evaluates default argument values exactly once, when the `def` statement runs — not once per call. `tags=[]` creates a single list object that becomes the default for every future call omitting that argument, and because `.append()` mutates it in place, every call that relies on the default is silently accumulating into the same shared list rather than getting an isolated fresh one, which is exactly the kind of thing a single-call trace won't reveal.
feedback.return-type-inconsistent: The function does consistently return a list on every call shown here — the actual defect is about what's *in* that list across separate calls, not about the type of what's returned.
feedback.append-is-slow: Performance isn't the issue in this snippet at all — `list.append` is the normal, efficient way to add to a Python list. The defect is a correctness bug, not a speed one.

contentSections.flawExplanation: This is one of Python's most well-documented traps for exactly this reason: the code reads as completely idiomatic, and the bug only shows up across multiple calls, never within a single one — a single-call trace, done in isolation the way the first lesson's happy-path technique teaches, would show `add_tag('urgent')` correctly returning `['urgent']` and reveal nothing wrong. The fix is the standard one: default to `None` and create a fresh list inside the function body when it's `None`, so every call that doesn't pass its own list actually gets an isolated one.

contentSections.body: A function that mutates an object it was handed — including its own default arguments — can leave state changed for callers who never expected to share anything. Trace more than one call before trusting a function that touches anything mutable.

title: Loops that terminate, and loops that only usually terminate
description: A loop's exit condition is a claim about what will eventually become true. The claim can be wrong, or true only for the inputs it was tested against.

learningObjectives.text: Trace a loop's exit condition against a concrete input to confirm it will actually be reached, not just that it's syntactically present
Identify a loop that terminates for typical inputs but has a reachable input for which it wouldn't

contentSections.title: "It has a break statement" is not the same as "it terminates"

contentSections.body:
```python
def find_available_username(base_name, is_taken_fn):
    candidate = base_name
    suffix = 1
    while is_taken_fn(candidate):
        candidate = f"{base_name}{suffix}"
        suffix += 1
    return candidate
```

This has no explicit `break` — it relies entirely on `is_taken_fn(candidate)` eventually returning `False`. That's a real, load-bearing assumption: it terminates if and only if there exists some suffix for which the username is available. For a real user-facing signup system, is that guaranteed? What if `is_taken_fn` is buggy and always returns `True`? What if every one of the first ten thousand suffixes is genuinely already taken by bots?

A loop terminates when its exit condition becomes true, and 'has an exit condition' is not the same claim as 'the exit condition is guaranteed to become true.' Reading a loop for correctness means tracing not just what the loop does on each pass, but what specifically would have to be true about the real world for the loop to ever stop — and then asking whether that thing is actually guaranteed, or just usually the case in the inputs anyone happened to test with.

This distinction matters because a loop that terminates for every test case anyone ran can still be an infinite loop waiting for the one input where the exit condition's assumption doesn't hold. `find_available_username` will terminate instantly in every manual test, because manually you'll never generate ten thousand taken usernames — but it has no upper bound, no maximum attempt count, and no fallback if the assumption 'eventually some suffix is free' turns out false or just extremely slow to become true in a specific adversarial or degenerate case.

The habit: for any loop without an explicit, counted bound (a `for i in range(n)`, a fixed retry count), name out loud what has to become true for the loop to exit, and ask specifically whether that's guaranteed by something in the code, or just an assumption about the data the loop expects to see.

contentSections.scenario:
A generated retry function:

```python
def fetch_with_retry(url, fetch_fn):
    response = None
    while response is None or response.status_code >= 500:
        response = fetch_fn(url)
    return response
```

No maximum attempt count anywhere in the function.
contentSections.question: If the remote server has an outage and returns a 503 status on every single request indefinitely, how many times will this loop call `fetch_fn` before returning — give your best estimate as a specific number.
contentSections.explanation: There's no finite correct number — that's the point of the exercise. The loop's exit condition, `response.status_code < 500`, depends entirely on the remote server eventually returning a non-5xx status, which is exactly the thing that isn't guaranteed during a real outage. With no maximum attempt count and no growing delay between attempts, a genuine prolonged outage turns this into an unbounded busy-loop, hammering the failing server with retries as fast as the loop can execute, for as long as the outage lasts — potentially forever, and actively making the outage worse by adding retry traffic to an already-failing service. A defensible version needs a maximum attempt count, and normally an increasing delay between attempts (the actual 'exponential backoff' the earlier module's stale comment claimed but never implemented).

contentSections.body: Name what specifically has to become true for a loop to exit, and check whether that's actually guaranteed by the code — a loop that terminates in every test you happened to run can still have no real upper bound.

contentSections.title: Mutating the thing you're iterating over

contentSections.body:
A second, more specific way a loop's termination assumption can quietly break: the loop mutates the very collection it's iterating over, changing the thing the loop's own progress is measured against while it's still measuring it. This can produce loops that skip elements, process elements twice, or in some languages and cases, throw an error mid-iteration or loop far longer than the original collection's length would suggest.

This is worth specifically watching for in generated code because 'iterate over a list, removing items that match some condition' is a common enough task that a model reaches for the intuitive-looking version — a `for` loop with a `.remove()` or `del` inside it — which looks correct, runs without crashing in simple manual tests, and quietly skips elements the moment two matching items sit next to each other in the list.

contentSections.question: What actually happens, and why does it happen specifically when two expired items are adjacent?

options.label: Removing an item shifts every later item one position earlier in the list, but the loop's internal position counter keeps advancing regardless — so the item that shifted into the just-vacated slot gets skipped entirely on the next pass
Python always raises a RuntimeError immediately when you call `.remove()` inside a `for` loop over the same list
This works correctly for this input — removal during iteration is only a problem when removing from the end of the list

feedback.index-shift-skip: Right. When the first expired item is removed, everything after it shifts one index to the left — the second expired item, previously at index 1, is now at index 0. But the loop's internal iterator has already advanced to look at index 1 next, which is now the *non-expired* item that shifted into that slot. The second expired item, now sitting at index 0, is never visited again. It survives the function despite matching the exact condition the loop was written to remove.
feedback.raises-exception: Python doesn't reliably raise an error for `list.remove()` during a `for` loop over that same list the way it does for some other mutate-while-iterating patterns — this specific case fails silently, by skipping, which is arguably worse than an exception because nothing signals that anything went wrong at all.
feedback.works-fine-here: This is exactly backwards — adjacency is precisely what triggers the bug. A single isolated expired item surrounded by non-expired items would in fact get removed correctly; it's specifically two (or more) expired items next to each other where the index shift causes one of them to be skipped.

contentSections.mechanism: Iteration position and list contents are two separate things that a `for` loop over a mutable list assumes stay in sync — remove an item mid-iteration and they don't. The loop's notion of 'next position' doesn't know the list just got shorter, so it silently skips whatever slid into the gap. The safe pattern is to iterate over a copy (`for item in list(items):`) or build a new list of survivors (`items = [i for i in items if not i.is_expired]`) rather than mutating the collection the loop itself is walking.

contentSections.body: A loop's progress and the collection it's iterating over need to stay in sync for the loop's own bookkeeping to mean what it claims — mutating the collection mid-iteration is a common, quiet way that assumption breaks.
