title: Why tools add libraries you didn't ask for
description: A model reaches for a familiar library the same way it reaches for a familiar variable name — because it's a common pattern in the code it learned from, not because it weighed the alternative of six lines of standard-library code.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why a generated diff reaches for a dependency for a task that standard-library code could handle in a few lines
Recognize the specific shape of an unnecessary dependency addition in a diff

contentSections.title: One function call, one new dependency

contentSections.body:
A model generating code is pattern-completing from an enormous amount of real code it's seen, and `import _ from 'lodash'` followed by a `_.pick` call is an extremely common pattern in that training data — lodash has been one of the most-imported packages in the JavaScript ecosystem for years, used constantly, including for tasks the language itself has since grown a native way to do. The model isn't weighing 'dependency versus six lines of standard library' as a tradeoff the way a careful human reviewer would; it's producing the statistically familiar shape of code for this kind of task, and the familiar shape, for a lot of common utility work, happens to include a well-known library.

This matters because the choice to add a dependency is a real decision with real, ongoing cost — install size, attack surface, a version to keep updated, a license to track — and a model reaching for a library isn't making that tradeoff consciously any more than it's consciously deciding a variable should be named `result` versus `output`. It's the most likely next token given everything it's seen, and 'the most statistically common way to write this' and 'the way that's actually best for this specific project' are not guaranteed to be the same thing, especially for a project that cares about bundle size, or already has a policy against adding new dependencies for one-off utility functions.

The practical habit: when a diff adds a new dependency for a task that's genuinely small, ask what the standard library or the language's own newer features would take to do the same thing — not because dependencies are always wrong, but because the model didn't actually make that comparison, and someone needs to.

contentSections.scenario: Four generated diffs, each adding exactly one new npm dependency for one specific task.
contentSections.question: Which of these is the clearest case of a dependency added for a task the language's own current features already handle well, with no real benefit from the package?

options.label: `import isEqual from 'lodash.isequal'` to deep-compare two plain objects, where `structuredClone` and manual comparison, or even `JSON.stringify` equality for simple cases, were viable, well-understood native alternatives for this specific use
`import { z } from 'zod'` to validate the shape of an incoming webhook payload with several required and optional fields, nested objects, and specific string formats
`import dayjs from 'dayjs'` to handle timezone-aware date arithmetic across a dozen different call sites in a scheduling application

feedback.deep-equal-native-alternative: Right — a deep-equality check for plain objects is a small, well-scoped, one-purpose task that JavaScript's own tools (or even a short hand-written recursive function) cover reasonably well for most cases, without pulling in a new external dependency and its own maintenance burden for something this narrow.
feedback.zod-for-validation: Runtime schema validation with nested shapes, optional fields, and format checks is exactly the kind of task that's genuinely painful and error-prone to hand-roll correctly — a validation library earns its place here by doing something meaningfully harder than a few lines of manual `if` checks would reliably do.
feedback.dayjs-for-scheduling: Timezone-aware date arithmetic, used repeatedly across many call sites, is a classic case where JavaScript's native `Date` is genuinely difficult to use correctly and consistently — a well-chosen date library is solving a real, recurring, error-prone problem, not just avoiding six lines of code.

contentSections.concept: The question isn't 'does this task have a library for it' — almost everything does. It's whether the task is genuinely hard or error-prone to do correctly by hand, repeated often enough to be worth abstracting, versus a small, one-off utility a few lines of plain language code would handle just as well, where the dependency is pure overhead the model added out of statistical habit rather than necessity.

contentSections.body: A model reaches for a familiar library because it's statistically common in code like this, not because it weighed the dependency's cost against a few lines of standard-library code — that comparison is still someone's job.

contentSections.title: The tell in the diff

contentSections.body:
There's a specific, reliable tell for spotting an unnecessary dependency in a generated diff: a new import used exactly once, for a single function call, doing something the surrounding language already has a built-in or near-trivial way to express. A library genuinely earning its place in a project tends to show up in multiple places, or handle something with real edge-case complexity underneath a simple-looking call — date libraries handling timezone and daylight-saving edge cases, validation libraries handling nested optional fields, HTTP client libraries handling retries and cancellation.

The other tell worth watching for: a dependency added to solve a problem that's actually about *unfamiliarity* with a language feature that already shipped, rather than a genuine gap. JavaScript's `structuredClone`, optional chaining, nullish coalescing, and array methods like `.flatMap()` and `.at()` are all relatively recent enough that a lot of training data predates them, which means a model can reach for a small utility library to do something a current runtime's native syntax already covers cleanly — not because the library is wrong, but because the built-in alternative simply wasn't as common in what it learned from.

contentSections.question: One of these two imports is well-justified; the other is a single-use import for something the language already handles natively. Which is which, and why?

options.label: `uuid` is justified — generating a cryptographically sound, correctly-formatted v4 UUID by hand is genuinely fiddly and easy to get subtly wrong. `lodash.isempty` is not — `items.length === 0` (for an array, which this clearly is) does the identical job in one native, obvious expression
Both are justified — UUIDs and emptiness checks are both common enough operations to warrant a dedicated, well-tested library each
Neither is justified — both should be replaced with hand-written equivalents

feedback.uuid-justified-isempty-not: Right. `uuid` is solving something with real, easy-to-get-wrong complexity underneath a simple call — correct entropy, correct version bits, correct formatting — where a hand-rolled version risks subtly non-random or malformed IDs. `isEmpty` on a known array is doing the job of `items.length === 0`, one native property check, with zero benefit from the abstraction and one more dependency (plus lodash's broader ecosystem baggage, even in its modular per-function form) for no real gain.
feedback.both-justified: Treating every utility call as equally justified misses the actual distinguishing question this lesson is built around: is the underlying task genuinely hard to get right by hand, or is the library just standing in for a native one-liner?
feedback.neither-justified: Correct UUID generation is exactly the kind of task worth pulling in a dedicated, audited library for — hand-rolling randomness and version-bit formatting correctly is a real source of subtle bugs, unlike checking whether an array's length is zero.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The `isEmpty` import is the unjustified one: for a known array (`items`), `items.length === 0` is exactly as correct, more explicit about what's actually being checked, and removes a dependency whose only job here was standing in for a property access. `lodash.isempty`'s real value — handling emptiness checks uniformly across arrays, objects, strings, Maps, and Sets — isn't being used at all in a context where the input type is already known and fixed.

contentSections.body: A single-use import doing something the language already expresses natively in one line is the clearest tell of an unnecessary dependency — check what the built-in alternative would actually cost before accepting the library.

title: Reading a package before you install it
description: A package's README tells you what it claims to do. Its download count, publish history, maintainer count, and dependency tree tell you what happens if that claim turns out to matter less than whether it's still cared for.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the specific, checkable signals that predict a package's ongoing reliability and maintenance, beyond its README
Distinguish a package worth trusting for a given task from one that merely looks polished

contentSections.title: The README is marketing. The registry page is evidence.

contentSections.body: A generated diff adds `import { parseCSV } from 'csv-magic'` for a one-time data-import script. The README, if you were to look, reads well: clean examples, a friendly tone, a badge claiming 100% test coverage. None of that tells you what actually matters before you run `npm install` and let this package's code execute in your project: when was it last published, how many other packages does it pull in transitively, is there more than one person who could plausibly fix a bug in it, and how many people are actually depending on it in production right now, which is a rough proxy for how many eyes would notice if something in it broke or turned malicious.

A README is written by the package's author to make a case for using it — it's fair to read, but it's not neutral evidence, the same way a function's docstring is a claim rather than a fact. The registry page (npm, PyPI, crates.io, whichever ecosystem) carries a different, more checkable kind of information, most of it visible in under a minute: **last publish date** (a package untouched for three years might be stable and finished, or might be abandoned — worth checking which by skimming its issue tracker for anything alarming and unaddressed), **weekly download count** (a rough, imperfect proxy for how battle-tested it is against real-world usage, and how many other projects would notice and report a regression), **number of maintainers** (a project with one listed maintainer is one person's account compromise, one person's burnout, or one person's changed priorities away from a maintenance gap), and **transitive dependency count** (every dependency this package pulls in is a dependency your project now has too, with its own maintenance status you didn't individually check).

None of these signals is decisive alone. A single-maintainer package can be perfectly fine for years; a heavily-downloaded package can still have a supply-chain incident. The habit is to actually look at more than one signal together before installing, rather than judging a package purely by whether its README reads well and its API looks clean — polish in documentation and reliability in maintenance are produced by different things and don't reliably correlate.

contentSections.scenario: You're evaluating `csv-magic` before adding it for a one-time import script. Its registry page shows: last published 3 years ago, 4,200 weekly downloads, one listed maintainer, 14 transitive dependencies, and an open issue from 18 months ago titled 'crashes on files with BOM' with no maintainer reply.
contentSections.question: Select every signal here that's genuinely relevant to whether you should trust this specific package for this specific task.

items.label: The unaddressed, 18-month-old bug report — a specific, concrete signal that a real, plausible failure mode (BOM handling, common in real-world CSV files) exists and nobody's fixing it
One listed maintainer, combined with the stale publish date — together they suggest this package may no longer be actively watched, which matters if you hit a bug or a security issue
4,200 weekly downloads in isolation, without comparing it to any alternative package's download count
14 transitive dependencies, for a script that will run once, by you, on your own machine, and never again

explanation.stale-unaddressed-issue: This is the single most concrete, task-relevant piece of evidence here — a specific, plausible failure mode, already reported, already unaddressed for over a year. For a CSV import task, BOM handling is a genuinely common real-world edge case, not an obscure one.
explanation.single-maintainer: Combined with a three-year-old last publish, this is a real signal about ongoing support, not a standalone red flag — a lot of genuinely fine packages have one maintainer and haven't needed a publish in years because they're simply done. It's the combination with the unaddressed issue that's the actual concern.
explanation.download-count-alone: 4,200 weekly downloads means very little without a comparison point — is that high or low for this category of package? Without knowing what a typical CSV-parsing library's download count looks like, this number alone doesn't tell you much either way.
explanation.transitive-deps-for-oneoff: 14 transitive dependencies matters a lot for a package that's going into a production application's long-term dependency tree — it matters far less for a script you're going to run once, locally, and delete. Context about how the package will actually be used changes whether a real signal is actually relevant here.

contentSections.synthesis: The signals that matter are the ones connected to the actual, specific risk for this specific use — a concrete unaddressed bug that's plausible for your data is real evidence; a raw download number with no comparison point isn't; and a signal's weight changes with context, like transitive dependency count mattering far less for a disposable script than for a long-lived service.

contentSections.body: A README is a claim made by the package's author. Publish recency, maintainer count, and unaddressed issues relevant to your actual use case are checkable evidence — read both, and weight the evidence by how relevant it is to your specific situation.

contentSections.title: Bus factor and the single point of failure

contentSections.body:
"Bus factor" — how many people would need to become unavailable before a project stalls — is worth naming explicitly for any dependency doing something load-bearing in a project meant to last. A package maintained by one person, however skilled and well-intentioned, is one account compromise, one burnout, one shift in priorities away from a maintenance gap nobody in your project controls or can predict. This isn't a criticism of solo maintainers, many of whom do excellent, careful work — it's a fact about risk distribution that's worth weighing against how load-bearing the package actually is in your system.

The practical calibration: a single-maintainer package doing something small, replaceable, and non-critical (a formatting utility, a one-off script dependency) carries low real risk even with a bus factor of one, because if it stalls, swapping it out is cheap. The same bus factor on a package your authentication flow, your payment processing, or your core data pipeline depends on is a meaningfully bigger risk, worth either a more heavily-maintained alternative or, at minimum, a deliberate note that this dependency's health is worth periodically checking.

contentSections.scenario: Two generated diffs on the same day. Diff A adds a single-maintainer package for pretty-printing debug output during local development only, never shipped to production. Diff B adds a different single-maintainer package for parsing and validating incoming webhook signatures — a security-critical step that runs on every production request.
contentSections.question: Why does the same bus-factor risk (one maintainer) warrant very different levels of concern across these two diffs?

options.label: The risk from a stalled maintainer is proportional to how load-bearing and how hard-to-replace the dependency is — a dev-only formatting tool is cheap to swap or drop if it stalls, while an unmaintained webhook-signature validator sitting on the security-critical path of every production request is a much more consequential single point of failure
Bus factor doesn't actually matter for either — what matters is only whether the package currently works correctly
Both diffs should be rejected outright, since single-maintainer packages should never be used for anything

feedback.criticality-differs: Right. The same underlying risk factor — one person's availability — has a very different consequence depending on what the package is actually load-bearing for. A dev-only tool stalling is an inconvenience; a security-critical validation library stalling, with an undiscovered bug or a missed CVE patch, is a real production risk. Bus factor isn't a fixed verdict, it's an input that needs to be weighed against what the dependency is actually doing.
feedback.bus-factor-irrelevant: Whether a package currently works is a snapshot in time — bus factor is specifically about the risk that it *stops* being maintained, patched, or fixed going forward, which matters more the more critical and long-lived the thing depending on it is.
feedback.always-avoid-single-maintainer: This ignores that a huge amount of genuinely excellent, widely-used open-source software is maintained by one person — the point isn't to categorically avoid solo-maintained packages, it's to weigh that risk against how critical and hard-to-replace the specific use is.

contentSections.mechanism: Bus factor is a probability of future disruption, not a verdict about current quality — and the actual cost of that disruption scales with how deeply embedded and how safety-critical the dependency is. The same input (one maintainer) produces a low-stakes risk for a swappable dev tool and a genuinely serious one for something sitting on a security-critical, hard-to-quickly-replace path.

contentSections.body: Bus factor is a real signal, but its weight depends entirely on what the dependency is actually load-bearing for — the same single-maintainer risk is trivial for a swappable dev tool and serious for something on a critical, hard-to-replace path.

title: Licences, and the ones that follow your code out the door
description: A permissive license lets you use a package and forget about it. A copyleft license is a condition attached to your own code, triggered by how you use theirs — and it doesn't announce itself in the README's code examples.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish permissive licenses from copyleft licenses by what obligation each places on code that depends on them
Identify a license whose obligations are triggered by the specific way a dependency is used in a given project

contentSections.title: Two questions a license actually answers

contentSections.body: A generated diff adds a well-regarded image-processing library to a proprietary SaaS product's backend. It works perfectly, passes every test, ships. Nobody on the team checked the license field in its `package.json` — `AGPL-3.0`. The AGPL's specific, unusual condition: if you run AGPL-licensed code as part of a service other people interact with over a network, you're obligated to make the *complete source code of your whole service* available to those users, not just the library itself. A perfectly working, well-tested feature just became a legal question for the company's lawyers, and the answer to 'should we have used this' was fully knowable before a single line was merged — it just needed someone to read one field.

A software license answers two questions worth separating clearly: what are you allowed to *do* with this code, and what does using it *obligate you to do* with your own code as a result. Permissive licenses (MIT, Apache 2.0, BSD variants) answer the second question with essentially nothing — use it, modify it, ship it inside proprietary software, no obligation to share your own source in return, beyond keeping the license notice attached to the library itself. This is why permissive-licensed packages are the overwhelming majority of what shows up in most commercial codebases without anyone thinking twice.

Copyleft licenses (GPL, LGPL, and especially AGPL) answer the second question very differently: using the code under certain conditions obligates you to release your own code — sometimes just the parts that directly link to the library, sometimes, in the AGPL's case, your whole running service — under the same license. The specific condition that triggers this obligation varies by license family and is exactly the kind of detail that doesn't show up in a code example or a README's quick-start section, only in the actual license text.

The practical habit: check the license field before merging a new dependency, not after — it's usually one line in a `package.json`, `pyproject.toml`, or the package's registry page, and it's the cheapest check in this entire module relative to how expensive getting it wrong can be for a company.

contentSections.scenario: Four generated diffs, each adding a package with a different license, to a proprietary, closed-source commercial product.
contentSections.question: Which license triggers a real, concrete obligation on the rest of this proprietary product's source code, given that the product is a network service other people log into and use?

options.label: `MIT` for a small string-formatting utility
`AGPL-3.0` for a data-visualization component rendered directly in the product's web dashboard, which every user's browser loads and runs as part of using the service
`Apache-2.0` for a logging library used internally

feedback.agpl-dashboard: Right. The AGPL's defining, unusual clause specifically covers software made available as a network service — exactly this product's situation — and its condition is triggered by users interacting with the software over a network, not by whether the code is literally redistributed as a file. A component embedded in the dashboard every user's browser runs is squarely inside that condition.
feedback.mit-formatting: MIT places essentially no obligation on the code that uses it — it can be embedded in fully proprietary, closed-source software with nothing more required than keeping the MIT license notice attached to the library's own files.
feedback.apache-logging: Apache 2.0 is also permissive, similar in practical effect to MIT for this purpose (with some added patent-grant language) — using it in proprietary internal tooling carries no obligation to release any of your own code.

contentSections.concept: The AGPL is specifically designed to close a gap the regular GPL doesn't cover: software run only as a network service, never literally distributed to end users as a copy of the code, was historically outside the GPL's trigger condition entirely — which the AGPL was written specifically to fix. It's the license most worth checking for explicitly in any product that's a service someone logs into, which describes most modern SaaS products, including most AI-assisted-development output.

contentSections.body: Permissive licenses (MIT, Apache 2.0, BSD) place essentially no obligation on your own code. Copyleft licenses, especially AGPL, can — and the trigger condition is specific enough that it's worth actually reading, not assuming from a package's popularity or polish.

contentSections.title: A model has no way to know your license policy

contentSections.body:
A generated diff choosing between two functionally similar packages has no visibility into which one is licensed permissively and which isn't, unless it's specifically asked to check — and even if it were shown both licenses, it has no way to know your company's actual policy (many companies flatly disallow GPL-family dependencies in proprietary products regardless of the specific trigger condition, as a simplifying, risk-averse rule). This is a decision that requires context the generation step structurally doesn't have: your product's business model, whether it's open-source itself, and your legal team's actual risk tolerance.

The practical review habit closing this lesson: treat a new dependency's license field as a required line item to check on every diff that adds one, the same reflexive way you'd check for a hardcoded secret — not because most dependencies turn out to be a problem (most are permissively licensed and entirely fine), but because the ones that aren't are expensive enough, and invisible enough in a typical code review, that skipping the check is a bad trade even at low odds.

contentSections.scenario: A study of the most popular npm packages found the overwhelming majority use permissive licenses (MIT, ISC, Apache-2.0, BSD), with copyleft-family licenses (GPL, LGPL, AGPL) making up a small minority.
contentSections.question: Out of the top 1,000 most-downloaded npm packages, roughly what percentage would you guess use a copyleft license (GPL/LGPL/AGPL family) rather than a permissive one?
contentSections.explanation: The real figure is small — commonly cited estimates put copyleft-licensed packages in the low single digits among the most popular npm packages, with the overwhelming majority permissively licensed. The point of the exercise isn't the exact number — it's that a low base rate is exactly why the check gets skipped by habit ('it's probably fine, most packages are') and exactly why skipping it is still a bad trade: a rare event with a large cost, that takes seconds to check for, doesn't stop being worth checking just because it's rare. The AGPL invoice-processing scenario from the hook is a low-probability, high-cost event — precisely the shape of risk a cheap, reflexive check is designed to catch.

contentSections.body: Most packages are permissively licensed, which is exactly why the license check gets skipped out of habit — and exactly why a rare, low-cost check against a rare, high-cost outcome is still worth doing on every new dependency, not just the ones that feel risky.

title: Packages that don't exist: hallucinated imports and the squatters waiting for them
description: A model can generate a plausible-sounding package name for a real need, with a confident import statement and realistic-looking usage — and nothing about how fluent it looks tells you whether the package is real.

learningObjectives.text: Explain the mechanism by which a model produces a confident, plausible-looking import for a package that doesn't exist
Identify the specific security risk created when a hallucinated package name is later published by someone else

contentSections.title: A plausible name is not a real package

contentSections.body:
A generated diff, asked to add retry logic with exponential backoff to an HTTP client:

```python
from requests_retry_toolkit import RetryingSession

session = RetryingSession(max_retries=3, backoff_factor=2)
```

`requests_retry_toolkit` sounds exactly like a real package — it's named the way real packages in this space are named, the API reads like a real API, and it's used with total confidence, no hedging, no comment saying 'verify this exists.' It doesn't exist. Running `pip install requests_retry_toolkit` today either fails outright, or — and this is the actual danger — succeeds, because someone registered that exact name after noticing models kept hallucinating it, and published something under it.

A model generating an import statement is doing the same thing it does generating a function name or a docstring: producing the most statistically plausible continuation, given the surrounding context, of what a package for this task would probably be called. For extremely common, real packages, this works fine — the model has seen `import requests` and `import numpy` so many times that it reliably reproduces them correctly. For less common needs, or oddly specific combinations, the model can produce a name that fits the *pattern* of real package names in that ecosystem perfectly, with fluent, confident usage code around it, without that specific package actually existing anywhere — the same fluency-without-correctness gap the earlier module on reading generated code for intent identified in comments and docstrings, here applied to an import statement instead.

This is a known, named phenomenon in AI-assisted development, sometimes called *package hallucination* or, once the security angle is included, *slopsquatting* — a play on 'typosquatting,' the older, well-known attack where someone registers `reqeusts` (a common typo of `requests`) hoping for accidental installs. Slopsquatting is the same idea with a different source of the mistake: instead of hoping for a human's typo, an attacker registers a name that AI tools have been observed hallucinating repeatedly, and waits for someone to run the generated install command without checking first.

The practical stakes: a package name that doesn't exist yet is not automatically safe just because installing it currently fails. It's a name that a real attacker can watch for — hallucination patterns are researchable and somewhat predictable — and claim at any point, turning a future `pip install` or `npm install` of the exact command a generated diff suggested into a supply-chain compromise, with malicious code executing inside your project the moment the install finishes.

contentSections.scenario: Six months after a generated diff suggested `pip install requests_retry_toolkit`, a security researcher discovers a package by that exact name was published to PyPI two months ago, containing code that exfiltrates environment variables on import.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism that made this attack possible, distinct from an ordinary malicious-package upload?

options.label: The model's hallucinated package name — reused across many developers' AI-assisted sessions asking for similar functionality — created a predictable, discoverable target name that an attacker could specifically watch for and register, rather than needing to guess or typo-squat an existing name
This happened purely because PyPI doesn't review package contents before publishing, which is true of any malicious package regardless of how its name was chosen
The developer should have simply known Python well enough to recognize the package name was fake on sight

feedback.hallucination-created-predictable-target: Right. The distinguishing mechanism of slopsquatting specifically is that the *target name itself* is discoverable in advance, because models tend to hallucinate the same or similar plausible names repeatedly for similar requests — an attacker doesn't need to guess a typo, they can research what AI tools actually suggest and register exactly that.
feedback.pypi-has-no-review: Lack of pre-publish review is a real, general fact about most package registries and a necessary precondition for any malicious upload — but it doesn't explain what's specific to slopsquatting versus any other malicious package, which is the predictability of the target name.
feedback.user-should-have-known-python: Package names in a large, actively-growing ecosystem are genuinely hard to verify from familiarity alone — plenty of real, legitimate, useful packages have names an experienced developer wouldn't recognize on sight either, which is exactly why 'sounds plausible' isn't a reliable signal in either direction.

contentSections.mechanism: The chain: a model hallucinates a plausible package name repeatedly, for a common enough request, that the specific name becomes a predictable, researchable target — an attacker identifies it, registers it with malicious code, and waits. The victim is anyone who ran the generated install command without first confirming the package exists on the real registry with a legitimate history — a verification step that takes seconds and that fluent, confident-looking generated code gives no visual signal is necessary.

contentSections.body: A confident, fluent import statement is exactly as easy for a model to generate for a package that doesn't exist as for one that does — verify a new package actually exists, on the real registry, with a real history, before running the install command a diff suggests.

contentSections.title: The check that closes this gap

contentSections.body:
The defense here is specific and cheap, worth stating as a concrete habit rather than a vague 'be careful': before running an install command a generated diff suggests for a package you haven't personally used before, open the actual registry page — npmjs.com, pypi.org, whichever ecosystem — and confirm the package exists, has a plausible publish history (not registered yesterday), and has a description and usage that actually match what the generated code is doing with it. This is the same registry-reading habit from earlier in this module, applied as a security gate rather than a quality gate — the two checks happen to be nearly the same motion.

The other half of the defense is noticing the shape of the risk in the first place: a hallucinated import is most likely for a less common task, an unusual combination of requirements, or a request phrased in a way that doesn't map cleanly onto one well-known package — exactly the situations where a generated diff is extrapolating furthest from its training data, and exactly where 'this looks fluent and confident' has the least actual connection to 'this is real.'

contentSections.question: Put these steps in the order you'd actually want to take before running an install command a generated diff suggests for an unfamiliar package.
steps: Notice the import is for a package you don't personally recognize or haven't used before
Open the package's actual page on the real registry (PyPI, npm, etc.) rather than trusting the diff's usage as proof it exists
Check that the package has a plausible publish history and isn't a brand-new, unknown registration
Confirm the package's actual documented purpose matches what the generated code is using it for
Only then run the install command
contentSections.explanation: The check has to happen before the install, not after — once a malicious package's install script has run, the compromise has already happened, since install scripts can execute arbitrary code on your machine. Verifying existence, publish history, and actual documented purpose (in that order, since existence is the first thing to confirm and purpose-matching is a finer-grained check once you know it's real) is what turns 'this looks plausible' into 'this is confirmed,' cheaply, before the risky step.

contentSections.body: Verify an unfamiliar package's existence and history on the real registry before installing, not after — the moment an install script runs is the moment a hallucinated-then-squatted package can compromise your machine.

title: The maintenance you inherit with every import
description: Every dependency you add is a piece of future work you've committed your project to, sight unseen — an upgrade you'll eventually need to do, a breaking change you'll eventually need to absorb, a security patch you'll eventually need to apply, on someone else's timeline.

learningObjectives.text: Name the specific, ongoing work a dependency commits a project to, beyond the moment it's installed
Weigh a dependency's ongoing maintenance cost against the cost of building and maintaining the equivalent functionality in-house

contentSections.title: Installing is the cheapest moment a dependency ever costs you

contentSections.body: `npm install some-package` takes about four seconds. What it actually commits a project to: a version to eventually bump, possibly across a breaking major-version change with its own migration guide to read; a security advisory to eventually respond to, on whatever schedule the maintainer discovers and discloses one; a transitive dependency tree that changes underneath you on every fresh install unless it's pinned; and, if the package is ever deprecated, abandoned, or removed from the registry entirely, a replacement to research and migrate to, on a timeline you didn't choose. The four-second install is the cheapest moment in that entire relationship.

A dependency isn't a one-time cost paid at install — it's a small, recurring claim on future attention for as long as the project depending on it exists. Every dependency added is a promise, implicit and easy to forget having made, that someone will eventually: read a changelog before upgrading, decide whether a breaking change actually affects this codebase, apply a security patch promptly enough to matter, and, in the worst case, replace the package entirely if it's abandoned or its incident history becomes disqualifying.

This cost scales with how many dependencies a project has, not linearly but closer to compounding — more dependencies means more version-bump decisions per week, more surface area for one of them to have a security advisory, and more transitive dependency conflicts between packages that each want a different version of some shared underlying library. A generated diff adding one more small, convenient dependency is adding one more small, ongoing claim on the team's future attention, and it's genuinely difficult to feel that cost in the moment a diff is being reviewed for correctness, because the cost is deferred and diffuse rather than immediate and visible.

The practical habit: when evaluating whether a new dependency is worth adding, explicitly ask not just 'does this work correctly right now' but 'am I willing to be the person who eventually upgrades this, reads its next breaking-change migration guide, and responds if it has a security advisory' — because for most small projects and small teams, that person is whoever's reviewing the diff today, whether or not they've thought about it that way.

contentSections.scenario: A small team is reviewing four dependencies a generated diff added across several PRs this month.
contentSections.question: Select every one where the ongoing maintenance burden is a real, worth-naming cost — not necessarily a reason to reject it, but a cost that should be weighed, not ignored.

items.label: A third-party authentication library handling password hashing and session tokens — security-critical, meaning any advisory needs a fast, prioritized response, not a 'get to it eventually'
A small CLI output-formatting library used only in an internal developer tool, never shipped to any customer or production system
A PDF-generation library used in a customer-facing billing feature, where a future breaking change could silently alter invoice layout if the upgrade isn't tested carefully
A mocking library used exclusively in the test suite, with no code path that ever runs in production

explanation.auth-library: Security-critical dependencies carry a genuinely different maintenance obligation than most — an advisory here needs prompt, prioritized attention, not the 'whenever someone gets to it' cadence that's fine for most routine dependency updates.
explanation.internal-cli-formatter: Low real cost: it's not customer-facing, not security-relevant, and if it's ever abandoned, swapping it for another formatting library or a hand-rolled version is cheap and low-risk, with no customer-facing consequence either way.
explanation.pdf-export: A breaking change here has a real, customer-visible failure mode (a malformed invoice) that could be easy to miss in casual testing — worth flagging as a dependency that needs deliberate, careful testing on every upgrade, not an automatic version bump.
explanation.test-only-mock-lib: Test-only dependencies that never run in production carry meaningfully lower risk — a security advisory in a test-only mocking library has no production attack surface, and a breaking change only affects developer workflow, not customers.

contentSections.synthesis: The maintenance cost that actually matters to name explicitly is concentrated in dependencies that are either security-relevant or customer-facing in a way where a breaking change could cause a silent, hard-to-notice regression — dev-only and test-only dependencies carry the same nominal 'someone will need to update this eventually' cost, but at meaningfully lower real stakes.

contentSections.body: A dependency's real cost is a small, recurring, easy-to-forget claim on future attention — weigh it heaviest for anything security-critical or customer-facing, where a missed update or an unnoticed breaking change actually costs something.

contentSections.title: What a supply-chain incident actually looks like

contentSections.body:
The sharpest version of this risk isn't a package quietly going stale — it's a widely-trusted, actively-used package's publishing account or maintainer getting compromised, and a malicious update going out under the same trusted name millions of projects already depend on. This has happened to real, extremely popular packages across ecosystems: a maintainer's credentials phished, a malicious version published, and every project that auto-updates or installs fresh without pinning a specific version pulling in the compromised code within hours, often before anyone notices.

This is precisely why the earlier lessons' evidence — maintainer count, publish history, how heavily-used and -watched a package is — matters beyond just predicting abandonment. A heavily-used package with an active community is more likely to have the compromise noticed and reverted quickly by someone else before you ever pull the malicious version; a small, quiet package with one maintainer and few users has no such safety net, and a compromise there could sit undiscovered far longer. None of this means dependencies are too risky to use — nearly all software depends on them, including software written by hand — it means the evaluation habits from this whole module (existence, maintenance signals, license, and now this) are worth applying together, not selectively, on anything a project genuinely depends on.

contentSections.question: A project pins every dependency to an exact version in its lockfile and only upgrades deliberately, reading changelogs first. A second, similar project auto-updates to the latest compatible version on every fresh install with no review step. Which is more exposed to a supply-chain compromise of a popular dependency, and why?
contentSections.hint: Think about the gap in time between a malicious version being published and it actually reaching a project's running code, in each setup.
contentSections.answer: The auto-updating project is more exposed — it pulls in a new version, potentially including a malicious one, the moment it's published and matches the version range, with no human review step in between to catch anything unusual before it's running in the codebase. The pinned project has a deliberate gap between a new version existing and it actually being adopted, during which a compromise is more likely to already be discovered, reported, and reverted by the wider community before this specific project ever installs it. Pinning isn't a complete defense — a deliberate upgrade can still adopt a compromised version if it happens to land during the review window — but it removes the fastest, most automatic path from 'malicious version published' to 'running in your project.'

contentSections.body: The evaluation habits from this whole module — existence, maintenance health, license, ongoing cost — exist together specifically because a supply-chain compromise is most dangerous for exactly the dependencies that skipped all of them: obscure, unpinned, unreviewed, and auto-updated.

contentSections.title: Seven drills

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Seven drills across the module's skills, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Do them in one sitting or spread across a few — nothing here expires.
If a drill needed a hint, that's what to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Audit the Dependency Additions in a Generated Pull Request
description: Take every new dependency a real or realistic PR adds, and produce a written keep/replace/remove call for each, backed by actual evidence.

learningObjectives.text: Apply necessity, registry-health, license, existence, and maintenance-cost evaluation to a real set of dependency additions
Produce a dependency review with a specific call and cited evidence per package, not a general impression

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Every lesson this module worked one dependency-evaluation habit at a time. A real pull request that adds several new packages needs all of them applied together, per package: is it necessary, is it healthy, what does its license obligate, does it actually exist with a real history, and what ongoing cost does it commit the project to. This lab produces the artefact a real dependency review actually looks like — a specific call per package, with evidence, not a blanket approval or rejection of the PR as a whole.

contentSections.title: Audit a PR's dependency additions
contentSections.brief: Find a real pull request — your own project's history, an open-source project's PR history, or one you generate now for a plausible feature (a CSV export, a notification system, an image upload pipeline) — that adds at least three new dependencies. If you can't find one with real dependency additions, construct a plausible one: list three to five packages a generated diff might add for a specific feature, with enough realistic detail (purpose, rough download count, license, last publish) to actually evaluate.
contentSections.deliverable: A dependency review: for each new package, a keep/replace/remove call, the specific evidence behind it (necessity, registry health, license, existence check, ongoing cost), and for anything marked replace or remove, what you'd use instead.

stages.title: List every new dependency and check necessity
stages.instructions: List every package the PR adds. For each, ask whether the task is genuinely hard enough to justify a dependency versus a few lines of code — mark any that fail this check as a likely 'replace with hand-written code' candidate before doing further evaluation on them.
stages.checkpoint: Every new dependency is listed, with an initial necessity call and a one-line reason.

stages.title: Check registry health and existence
stages.instructions: For each package that passed the necessity check, confirm it actually exists with a real publish history, and note its maintenance signals — last publish, maintainer count, any relevant open issues.
stages.checkpoint: Every remaining package has a documented existence check and maintenance-health summary.

stages.title: Check license and ongoing cost
stages.instructions: For each package, note its license and whether it creates any obligation given how this specific product runs (network service, distributed binary, internal tool). Then name the ongoing maintenance stakes — how critical is the path it sits on, who's responsible for upgrading it.
stages.checkpoint: Every package has a license note and an ongoing-cost assessment tied to its actual criticality.

stages.title: Write the final calls and the deliverable
stages.instructions: For each package, make a final keep/replace/remove call backed by the evidence gathered. For anything not kept as-is, state a specific alternative. Compress into the deliverable and self-check against the rubric.
stages.checkpoint: Every package has a specific call, cited evidence, and — where relevant — a named alternative, not a vague 'this seems risky.'

rubric.criterion: Every new dependency in the PR has an individual call, not a blanket verdict on the PR as a whole
rubric.meets: Each package is evaluated and called separately, even if several end up with the same verdict.

rubric.criterion: Each call is backed by specific, named evidence
rubric.meets: The reasoning cites an actual fact — a publish date, a license name, a specific missing standard-library alternative — not a general impression.

rubric.criterion: At least one necessity call is made explicitly, even if every package passes
rubric.meets: The 'could this be a few lines of code instead' question is asked and answered for every package, not skipped for the ones that seem obviously fine.

rubric.criterion: License is addressed for every package, even briefly
rubric.meets: Each package has a stated license and a one-line note on whether it's relevant given how this product runs — 'permissive, no concern' is a valid, sufficient answer when true.

rubric.criterion: Anything called replace or remove has a specific alternative named
rubric.meets: A rejection without a stated alternative isn't a complete review — the deliverable names what to use instead.

contentSections.body: A dependency review that says 'looks fine' about a whole PR is exactly as unfalsifiable as a code review that says the same about a whole diff — the useful version names each package, cites the specific evidence, and makes a call someone else could check.
