title: Tests as the only executable documentation you have
description: A comment can drift from the code without anyone noticing. A test that drifts from the code fails the build — which makes a passing test suite the one document in an undocumented codebase that's still provably true right now.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why a passing test carries a stronger correctness guarantee than a comment or a README, given how each stays or fails to stay true over time
Read a test file as a source of intent when no other documentation exists

contentSections.title: A comment can lie silently. A test can't.

contentSections.body:
No README, no ticket, no comment — just a function and its test file.

```python
def compute_late_fee(balance, days_late):
    ...

def test_compute_late_fee_caps_at_25_percent():
    fee = compute_late_fee(balance=1000, days_late=90)
    assert fee == 250
```

The function's implementation might have a stale comment above it, or no comment at all. The test can't drift the same way — it either currently passes, meaning `compute_late_fee(1000, 90)` really does return `250` right now, or it currently fails, which the whole team would already know about. A passing test is the one artifact in this codebase that's *mechanically checked to still be true*, every time the suite runs, with no possibility of quietly going stale the way a comment can.

The earlier module in this phase on reading for intent established that comments and docstrings are claims, not facts — written once, checked by nothing, free to drift from the code beneath them without anyone noticing. A test is a fundamentally different kind of claim: it's a claim the build actively re-verifies every time it runs, and if the claim stops being true, the test suite turns red and — in any team with even minimal process — someone notices before the code ships. This doesn't make a test a perfect description of intent (later lessons in this module cover exactly how a test can pass while checking almost nothing), but it does make a *passing* test meaningfully more trustworthy than a comment making the same claim, purely because of what would have to happen for it to be false: a comment can be false silently, forever; a test being false is, structurally, a build failure.

In an undocumented codebase — which describes a lot of real, especially newer AI-assisted codebases, where a comment explaining intent is easy to skip generating and a test is often the thing that actually got written to confirm a feature works — the test suite is frequently the *only* executable record of what the code is actually supposed to do. Reading test names, arrangements, and assertions as a primary source of intent, not an afterthought once you've already read the implementation, is a real, distinct skill from reading the implementation itself.

The habit this lesson opens with: when you land in unfamiliar code, check whether tests exist before assuming you need to read the implementation cold. A well-named test (`test_compute_late_fee_caps_at_25_percent`) can hand you the requirement — a fee that caps at 25% of the balance — faster than tracing the implementation's own branches would.

contentSections.scenario: You've just opened an unfamiliar module with no README and one stale, contradictory comment above a function. The module does have a test file alongside it.
contentSections.question: What's the most efficient first move, given the tools available?

options.label: Read the test file's test names and assertions first, to form a hypothesis about the requirement, before diving into the implementation's logic
Trust the stale comment, since it's presumably describing the original intent even if slightly outdated
Skip both and trace the implementation cold, since tests could also be wrong

feedback.tests-first: Right. A test that's currently passing is mechanically confirmed true right now, in a way a comment structurally can't be — reading it first gives you a verified starting hypothesis about the requirement, which then makes reading the implementation a confirmation pass rather than starting from nothing, the same efficiency gain the earlier module found in reading a function's signature before its body.
feedback.trust-comment: The lesson this hook opened with is specifically about why a comment can't be trusted the way a passing test can — a stale, contradictory comment is exactly the kind of claim that's had every opportunity to silently drift from the truth, unlike a test the build re-checks on every run.
feedback.implementation-cold: Tests can be wrong too, and this module's later lessons cover exactly how — but 'tests can also be imperfect' isn't a reason to skip the fastest, most-verified starting point available; it's a reason to read them critically rather than not at all.

contentSections.concept: A passing test is the one document in an otherwise undocumented codebase that's continuously, mechanically re-verified — reading it first, before the implementation, gives you a checked starting hypothesis instead of an unverified one, the same efficiency principle behind reading a signature before a function body.

contentSections.body: A passing test is re-verified every time the build runs, which a comment never is — read a test suite as your primary source of intent in undocumented code, before the implementation, not as an afterthought once you've already formed a guess.

contentSections.title: What a test file's shape tells you before you read a single assertion

contentSections.body:
Before reading individual assertions, a test file's overall shape is itself informative: how many tests exist for a given function, what their names describe, and which cases are covered by name alone. A function with one test named `test_compute_late_fee` tells you less than a function with four tests named `test_caps_at_25_percent`, `test_zero_for_paid_invoice`, `test_zero_when_not_yet_due`, and `test_rate_applies_per_day` — the second set is effectively a table of contents for the function's actual behavior, readable before a single line of the implementation.

This is worth checking specifically because the number and naming of tests for a piece of AI-generated code is itself a signal about how carefully it was built out, in a way that's cheap to read: a function with no tests at all is a function whose behavior you'll need to establish entirely through implementation-reading and your own manual tracing; a function with several specifically-named tests is one where someone (or some prompt) already thought through several of its distinct cases, and you can use their thinking as a starting map rather than building one from nothing.

contentSections.question: You find a function `apply_late_fee` with zero tests anywhere in the codebase, and a second function `calculate_shipping_cost` in the same file with six specifically-named tests covering different weight tiers, international shipping, and free-shipping thresholds. Before reading either implementation, which one would you expect to take longer to fully understand, and why?
contentSections.hint: One of these hands you a partial map of its behavior for free; the other hands you nothing.
contentSections.answer: `apply_late_fee`, almost certainly — with zero tests, there's no executable documentation at all, and understanding its full behavior requires reading the implementation cold and manually tracing every case yourself, the way the earlier module's techniques work without any test-derived head start. `calculate_shipping_cost`'s six specifically-named tests hand you a partial map of its behavior before you've read a line of its body: weight tiers, international handling, and a free-shipping threshold are all named cases you can now specifically look for in the implementation, turning that read into confirmation rather than open discovery — the same efficiency gain reading a signature and its returns provides, here scaled up by an entire test file's worth of named cases.

contentSections.body: A test file's names and count, read before any individual assertion, are a table of contents for a function's known behavior — a rich, specifically-named test file hands you a head start; an empty one hands you nothing, and tells you so honestly.

title: Reading a test to find the requirement behind it
description: A test's arrangement, action, and assertion are three separate claims — what situation was set up, what was actually done, and what was checked afterward — and the real requirement usually lives in the gap between the test's name and what it actually asserts.

learningObjectives.text: Decompose a test into its arrange/act/assert structure to extract the specific requirement it's checking
Identify when a test's name claims more than its actual assertion checks

contentSections.title: Arrange, act, assert — read all three separately

contentSections.body:
```python
def test_refund_within_window():
    order = Order(total=100, purchased_at=days_ago(10))
    result = process_refund(order)
    assert result.approved
    assert result.amount == 100
```

Read as one block, this looks like a simple confirmation. Decomposed: the *arrangement* fixes one specific fact — this order is exactly 10 days old — which is itself a claim about the boundary this test is probing, not an arbitrary number. The *action* calls the one function under test. The *assertion* checks two separate things: that a refund was approved at all, and that the amount is the full $100, not a partial refund. That second assertion is easy to skim past, and it's actually encoding a real requirement: a refund within the window is full, not prorated.

Every test worth reading for intent decomposes into three parts, and reading them as one undifferentiated block is how a real requirement hides in plain sight. The **arrangement** — the setup, the specific input values chosen — is itself a claim: a test that arranges `purchased_at=days_ago(10)` rather than `days_ago(1)` or `days_ago(29)` is very likely probing something specific about a boundary, not picking an arbitrary number, the same way this phase's earlier module treated a specific, non-round constant in implementation code as evidence of a deliberate decision. The **action** is usually the least informative part — it's just the call to the function under test. The **assertion** is where the actual requirement is stated, and it's worth reading assertion by assertion, not just noticing that assertions exist, because — as the hook showed — a second or third assertion can carry a distinct, easy-to-skim-past requirement of its own.

The specific habit for this lesson: for each assertion in a test, ask what real-world requirement would make this specific check necessary — not just 'the code returns true here,' but 'why does the test author care that it returns true specifically here, with these specific values.' A test asserting `result.amount == 100` isn't just confirming 'a number came back' — given a $100 order, it's confirming the refund is full-value, a genuine business rule (full refunds within the window, not prorated ones) that the assertion states more precisely than the test's own name does.

contentSections.problem:
Decompose this test and extract the specific requirement it encodes.

```python
def test_bulk_order_discount():
    cart = Cart(items=[Item(price=10, qty=15)])
    total = calculate_total(cart)
    assert total == pytest.approx(127.50)
```

steps.label: Read the arrangement
steps.work: One item, price $10, quantity 15. Fifteen units of a single $10 item — a specific, deliberately round-but-not-trivial quantity.
steps.why: 15 units suggests this is testing a bulk-discount threshold specifically — a quantity high enough to plausibly cross into a discount tier, not just an arbitrary cart contents choice.

steps.label: Compute what the total would be with NO discount
steps.why: This baseline is essential to interpreting the assertion — without it, `127.50` is just a number; with it, the gap between $150 and $127.50 becomes the actual finding.

steps.label: Read the assertion against that baseline
steps.work: $127.50 is $150 minus $22.50, which is exactly 15% off $150.
steps.why: The requirement this test actually encodes: a 15-unit order of this item receives a 15% discount. The test's name says 'bulk order discount' generically; the assertion, read against a computed baseline, states the specific rate.

faded.problem:
Decompose this second test the same way.

```python
def test_free_shipping_threshold():
    cart = Cart(items=[Item(price=25, qty=2)], destination='domestic')
    shipping = calculate_shipping(cart)
    assert shipping == 0
```

blanks.prompt: What's the cart's total value, computed from the arrangement?
blanks.why: As in the worked example, the assertion is only interpretable against a value computed from the arrangement, not read in isolation.

blanks.prompt: What specific requirement does `shipping == 0` encode, given that computed total?
blanks.answer: Domestic orders totaling $50 or more (or possibly exactly $50, depending on whether the threshold is inclusive) qualify for free shipping.
blanks.why: The test's name says 'free shipping threshold' generically; the specific number, $50, is the actual requirement, extracted only by computing the arrangement's total and reading it against the assertion.

blanks.prompt: What's one thing this single test does NOT tell you about the threshold, that you'd need a second test to confirm?
blanks.answer: Whether $50 is exactly the boundary (inclusive) or whether the real threshold is lower and $50 just clearly qualifies — a test with cart total exactly at $49.99 or some other near-boundary value would be needed to pin down the exact cutoff.
blanks.why: This is the same open-question habit from the earlier module's reconstruction lesson — a single data point supports an inference, but the exact boundary needs a boundary-probing test to actually confirm, not just imply.

contentSections.procedure: Read the arrangement for specific, deliberately-chosen values. Compute a baseline where relevant (what would this be without the behavior under test). Read the assertion against that baseline to extract the actual numeric or logical requirement — which is usually more specific than the test's name alone states.

contentSections.body: A test's arrangement, action, and assertion are three separate claims — the real requirement usually lives in reading the assertion against a computed baseline from the arrangement, not in the test's name alone.

contentSections.title: When the name promises more than the assertion checks

contentSections.body:
The gap runs the other direction too, and it's the more consequential one to catch: a test named for a broad requirement whose actual assertion checks something much narrower. `test_validates_email` that only asserts a function returns `False` for one specific malformed input tells you the function rejects *that* input — it says nothing about whether the function correctly accepts genuinely valid emails, or correctly rejects other malformed ones, despite a name that reads as a general claim about validation working correctly.

This is the test-reading version of the earlier module's name-versus-body distinction applied to comments and function names — a test's name is a claim made by whoever wrote it, generated by the same process (human or model) as the assertion itself, with nothing forcing the two to actually match in scope. Reading a test's name as proof the requirement is fully covered, without checking what the assertion specifically verifies, is exactly the kind of name-trusting mistake this whole phase has been building the habit of catching.

contentSections.question: The test name claims to cover 'invalid input' generally. What's the actual, narrower scope of what this test verifies?

options.label: It verifies exactly one thing: that the specific string `"abc"` returns `None`. It says nothing about negative numbers, empty strings, floats, extremely large numbers, or any other input that might also be 'invalid' but isn't `"abc"`
The name is accurate — testing one clearly-invalid string is a representative, sufficient check for 'handles invalid input' generally
The problem is that the assertion should check for a raised exception instead of a returned None

feedback.one-case-only: Right. This is a single data point wearing the clothing of a general claim. A non-numeric string is one specific kind of invalid input among many plausible ones — negative ages, ages of 200, empty strings, `None` itself passed in directly — and this test's actual, narrow assertion says nothing about how the function handles any of those.
feedback.name-matches-scope: One example is evidence for that one example, not for the general category — this is precisely the over-generalization the lesson is warning about, treating a test's name as though it guarantees coverage its actual assertion doesn't provide.
feedback.assertion-too-strict: Whether `None` or an exception is the right response design is a separate, legitimate question from this exercise's actual point, which is about the gap between the test's broad name and its narrow actual scope — that gap exists regardless of which specific failure behavior the function chooses.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A test named for a general category, backed by exactly one example, tells you the function handles that one example — full stop. Treating the name as proof the whole category is covered is exactly the kind of name-trusting error the earlier reading-for-intent module warned against for function names and comments, applied here to test names: a name is a claim by whoever wrote the test, not a guarantee about what the assertion beneath it actually checks.

contentSections.body: A test's name can claim a broader requirement than its assertion actually checks — read what's specifically asserted, against what specific arrangement, before trusting a name's implied scope.

title: Tests that pass because they assert nothing
description: A green checkmark next to a test's name means the assertions inside it didn't fail — it says nothing about whether those assertions were actually capable of catching a real bug.

learningObjectives.text: Identify a vacuous or tautological assertion that would pass regardless of whether the code under test is correct
Distinguish a test that exercises real behavior from one that only confirms the code ran without crashing

contentSections.title: "It ran without crashing" is not the same claim as "it's correct"

contentSections.body:
```python
def test_calculate_total():
    cart = Cart(items=[Item(price=10, qty=3)])
    total = calculate_total(cart)
    assert total is not None
```

This test is green. It will stay green if `calculate_total` returns `30` (correct), `0` (wrong), `-5` (very wrong), or `"thirty"` (a completely different type than expected) — every one of those values is 'not None,' so every one of them passes this assertion. The test ran the function, confirmed it didn't crash and didn't return the specific value `None`, and checked absolutely nothing about whether the actual computed total is right. A reviewer glancing at a green test suite and a passing CI badge has no way to see this from the outside — the checkmark looks identical whether the assertion is meaningful or vacuous.

A vacuous, or tautological, assertion is one that's structurally guaranteed — or near-guaranteed — to pass regardless of whether the code under test actually behaves correctly. `assert result is not None`, `assert response.status_code < 500` (passes for a 200, a 400, a 404 — nearly every plausible response short of a server error), `assert isinstance(result, dict)` (checks the type, never the contents), and `assert True` written as a placeholder that never got filled in are all common, real shapes this takes. Every one of them produces a genuine green checkmark, contributes to a genuine 'tests passing' CI status, and catches essentially no real bugs, because the space of wrong answers that would still satisfy the assertion is enormous.

This specific failure is worth naming as a distinct risk in AI-generated test suites: a model asked to 'add tests' for a function has a strong incentive, structurally, to produce something that passes — and the cheapest, most reliable way to guarantee a passing test is a weak assertion that's hard to violate, whether or not that was anyone's intention. A generated test suite that's 100% green can create a false sense of security disproportionate to how much it actually verified, precisely because the failure is invisible from the outside — a red test suite announces a problem; a suite full of vacuous-but-green tests announces nothing at all.

The reading habit: for every assertion, ask the specific question 'what wrong value would this assertion fail to catch?' If the honest answer is 'almost anything except a crash or a literal None,' the test is close to vacuous regardless of how confident its name sounds.

contentSections.scenario:
A generated function `apply_tax` has a bug: it multiplies by the tax rate as a percentage (e.g. `8.5`) instead of converting it to a decimal first (`0.085`), producing wildly inflated totals. Its accompanying test:

```python
def test_apply_tax():
    result = apply_tax(price=100, rate=8.5)
    assert result > 0
```

This test is green in CI.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism by which this genuine, serious bug ships with a fully green, passing test suite?

options.label: `assert result > 0` is satisfied by the correct answer (`$108.50`) and by the buggy answer (`$950`, from multiplying by 8.5 as a whole number) equally — the assertion's scope is so wide it can't distinguish correct from badly wrong, so the bug simply never has a chance to fail the test
This must mean the test runner itself has a configuration problem, since a real bug should always be caught by its accompanying test
The bug is actually in how `rate=8.5` is documented, not in the multiplication logic or the test

feedback.vacuous-assertion-cant-catch-it: Right. `result > 0` is true for the correct total and for a total roughly nine times too large — the assertion's pass condition is so wide that a genuinely severe bug (charging customers ten times the intended amount) sails through it without any resistance. This is what makes vacuous assertions dangerous rather than just unhelpful: they don't merely fail to add confidence, they actively manufacture false confidence in the form of a green checkmark.
feedback.test-runner-broken: There's no evidence of a runner or configuration problem here — the test genuinely, correctly executes, and its assertion genuinely, correctly evaluates to `True` for the buggy result. The failure is in what the test chose to check, not in any tooling malfunction.
feedback.tax-rate-ambiguous: The multiplication bug (treating a percentage like `8.5` as though it were already a decimal fraction) is a real, specific, and common category of bug — the point of this exercise isn't to relitigate the source of the bug, it's to see exactly why the test failed to catch a bug that specific and that severe.

contentSections.mechanism: A vacuous assertion has a pass condition wide enough to include both the correct behavior and a large space of incorrect behavior. The bug doesn't evade the test through any special cleverness — it simply falls inside the enormous region of results the assertion was never narrow enough to exclude in the first place. The fix is always the same: assert the actual expected value (`assert result == 108.50`), which a nine-times-too-large result would immediately and obviously fail.

contentSections.body: A vacuous assertion doesn't fail to help — it actively manufactures a false green checkmark, because its pass condition is wide enough to include both the correct answer and a large space of badly wrong ones.

contentSections.title: The other shape: tests that never reach the assertion at all

contentSections.body:
A second, related shape worth naming separately: a test that wraps its call in a broad `try/except` and only asserts inside the success branch, silently passing (or reporting nothing meaningful) if an exception is raised instead. This produces green not because the code is correct, but because the test's own structure never gives a wrong result the chance to be checked — it either checks a correct result, or it doesn't check anything at all, and both outcomes look identical from outside the test file.

The practical version of this to watch for in generated test code specifically: a broad exception handler added defensively 'just in case,' around test logic that was meant to be a strict check. It's an easy pattern for a model to produce, because 'handle exceptions gracefully' is a common, generally-good instinct in application code — applied to test code, where the entire point is that a failure should be loud and visible, the same instinct becomes actively counterproductive.

contentSections.scenario: Four generated test snippets.
contentSections.question: Select every one where the test's structure would allow a real, wrong result to pass silently — not just a weak assertion, but a test that might never actually reach a check at all.

items.label:
```python
try:
    result = risky_calculation()
    assert result == 42
except Exception:
    pass
```

```python
result = calculate_discount(100, 0.1)
assert result == 90
```

```python
try:
    process_payment(order)
except Exception:
    pytest.fail('should not raise')
# no assertion on the actual outcome after the try block
```

```python
result = get_user_status(user_id)
assert isinstance(result, str)
assert result in ('active', 'suspended', 'deleted')
```

explanation.try-except-pass: If `risky_calculation()` raises an exception for any reason — including a genuine bug that should be caught — the `except Exception: pass` silently swallows it, and the test reports as passed with the actual assertion (`result == 42`) never having been evaluated at all.
explanation.strict-equality: This asserts a specific, exact expected value with no escape hatch — any wrong result from `calculate_discount` fails this test loudly and specifically, exactly the shape of a meaningful assertion.
explanation.assert-not-raises-only: This test only ever checks that no exception was raised — it never asserts anything about whether the payment was actually processed correctly (the right amount, the right account, success recorded properly). A function that silently does nothing at all, without raising, would pass this test just as cleanly as a function that processes the payment perfectly.
explanation.type-and-value-check: This checks both the type and that the value is one of a specific, finite, meaningful set of valid outcomes — narrow enough that most wrong results (a typo'd status string, a None, a wrong type) would genuinely fail it, even though it doesn't pin down which exact status is expected for this specific user.

contentSections.synthesis: The dangerous shape isn't 'has a try/except' or 'checks a type' in isolation — it's a test structure where a real, wrong outcome has no path to actually failing the test, whether because an exception silently escapes the check, or because the only thing verified is 'didn't crash' rather than 'did the right thing.'

contentSections.body: A test that swallows exceptions before its assertion runs, or that only ever checks 'didn't crash,' can pass for a function that's silently doing nothing or doing the wrong thing — check whether a wrong outcome has any actual path to failing the test.

title: Mocks that make the test agree with the code, whatever the code does
description: A mock that stands in for a real dependency is only useful if it can disagree with the code under test — one that's built to always agree isn't testing anything, it's just watching itself nod.

learningObjectives.text: Identify a mock configured to always match whatever the code under test expects, regardless of whether that expectation is correct
Distinguish a test verifying real behavior from one verifying only that a mock was called in a particular way

contentSections.title: A mock that mirrors the code isn't checking the code

contentSections.body:
```python
def test_get_user_display_name(mocker):
    mock_db = mocker.patch('app.db.fetch_user')
    mock_db.return_value = {'first_name': 'Jordan', 'last_name': 'Lee'}
    result = get_user_display_name(user_id=1)
    assert result == 'Jordan Lee'
```

This looks like a normal, reasonable use of mocking — stub out the database, check the function's logic in isolation. Whether it's actually a good test depends entirely on one thing this snippet alone can't show you: does `get_user_display_name`'s real implementation genuinely combine `first_name` and `last_name` with a space, correctly, or did whoever wrote the mock's return value already know what the implementation does and construct a mock specifically shaped to make it pass? A mock that's built by reading the implementation first, rather than by reading the actual requirement first, risks becoming a mirror the code checks itself against rather than an independent check.

Mocking exists for a good reason: isolating a function from a real database, a real network call, or a real external service makes tests fast, deterministic, and independent of things outside your control. The risk this lesson is about isn't mocking itself — it's a mock configured with values chosen specifically to make the code under test pass, rather than values chosen to represent what a real dependency would actually, plausibly return, including its edge cases and its failure modes.

This risk is sharper in AI-generated test code for a specific, structural reason: a model asked to write a test for a function it just generated (or that's shown in the same context) has full visibility into that function's implementation, and producing a mock return value that happens to make the assertion pass is a much easier generation task than independently deriving what a real dependency's response actually looks like from its own documentation or contract. The result can be a test that's internally consistent — the mock and the code agree perfectly — while telling you nothing about whether either one is actually correct against the real world.

The reading habit: for any test using a mock, ask where the mock's return value came from. If it's traceable to the actual, documented shape of the real dependency's response — a real API's documented schema, a real database's actual column types — the mock is doing genuine work. If the mock's value seems to exist purely because it's exactly what makes this specific implementation's assertion pass, the test is closer to checking that the code agrees with itself than checking that the code is correct.

contentSections.scenario:
A generated function has a real bug: it expects a payment gateway's response to have a field called `transaction_id`, but the actual gateway's real, documented API returns the field named `txn_id`. Its test:

```python
def test_process_payment(mocker):
    mock_gateway = mocker.patch('app.gateway.charge')
    mock_gateway.return_value = {'transaction_id': 'tx_123', 'status': 'success'}
    result = process_payment(order)
    assert result.transaction_id == 'tx_123'
```

This test passes. The function fails in production against the real gateway.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism by which this test passes despite a genuine, production-breaking bug?

options.label: The mock's return value uses the field name `transaction_id` — matching the buggy code's expectation exactly, rather than `txn_id`, the real gateway's actual documented field name — so the test verifies the code agrees with a mock shaped like the bug, not that the code agrees with the real dependency
This must mean the real payment gateway recently changed its API and the test was written correctly against an older version
The bug is that the assertion checks `.transaction_id` instead of checking the raw dictionary directly

feedback.mock-shaped-to-match-bug: Right. The mock's field name was set to match what the buggy code expects, not what the real gateway actually returns — whether that happened because the mock was written by reading the (buggy) implementation rather than the gateway's real documentation, or because a model generating both the code and its test made the identical field-naming assumption in both places. Either way, the test verifies internal agreement between two things that share the same wrong assumption, which is worse than not testing at all, because it produces false confidence specifically at the exact point where the real bug lives.
feedback.gateway-changed-recently: Nothing in the scenario suggests an API version change — the scenario states this as the gateway's actual, current, documented field name, which the code simply never matched to begin with.
feedback.assertion-checks-wrong-field: The assertion syntax itself isn't the problem — `result.transaction_id` is a completely reasonable way to check a result object's attribute. The actual defect is upstream: the mock supplies a field name that doesn't match reality, and the code that reads it was never checked against what the real dependency provides.

contentSections.mechanism: When a mock's shape is derived from the code under test rather than from the real dependency's actual contract, the mock and the code can share the exact same wrong assumption — and a test comparing two things that agree with each other, rather than comparing the code against an independent, accurate stand-in for reality, cannot detect a bug that both of them share. This is the test-suite version of the earlier module's finding that a name and its docstring agreeing with each other proves nothing, since both come from the same generation pass.

contentSections.body: A mock's return value needs to come from the real dependency's actual, documented contract — not from reading the implementation and reverse-engineering whatever would make its assertion pass — or the test can only ever catch bugs the mock doesn't also share.

contentSections.title: Testing that a mock was called, versus testing the outcome

contentSections.body:
A related, narrower risk: a test that verifies a mock was *called*, with certain arguments, but never verifies anything about the actual downstream outcome or the function's return value. This is sometimes genuinely the right thing to check — confirming a specific side effect happened is a legitimate test, when the side effect itself is the entire point (did we call the payment gateway at all, did we log the event). It becomes a problem when it's the *only* thing checked, standing in for verifying the function's actual observable behavior.

The distinguishing question: is verifying the mock call a check on a genuine, meaningful side effect (an email really was requested to be sent, a payment really was requested to be charged), or is it a check on an implementation detail that happens to be how this particular version of the code is currently structured (this specific internal helper function was called, in this specific order) — something that would break the test on a legitimate refactor that changes *how* the function achieves the same correct outcome, without the outcome itself ever being wrong.

contentSections.question: What's the actual gap in what this test verifies?

options.label: It only confirms that an internal helper function was called once — it never checks the actual discounted total that `apply_discount` produces, so a version of the function that calls `_round_currency` correctly but computes a completely wrong discount amount would still pass this test
`assert_called_once()` is the wrong method — it should be `assert_called()` instead
This is a perfectly sufficient test of the discount logic

feedback.checks-internal-call-not-outcome: Right. This test checks a private implementation detail — that a specific internal helper got called exactly once — and says nothing whatsoever about the actual value `apply_discount` produces. A version of the function with a completely wrong discount percentage, or a wrong base price, would call `_round_currency` exactly once regardless, and this test would still pass.
feedback.mock-called-once-is-wrong-assertion: The specific assertion method isn't the problem — whether it's `assert_called()` or `assert_called_once()`, both are checking the same category of thing (was an internal function invoked), not the actual computed result, which is the real gap.
feedback.test-is-fine: This test provides essentially no coverage of the discount calculation's correctness — it's checking an implementation detail (a private helper was invoked) rather than the actual, observable outcome (the discounted total), which is what a caller of `apply_discount` actually cares about.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A meaningful version of this test would call `apply_discount(cart, 0.1)` and assert on its actual return value or the cart's resulting total — not on whether an internal, private helper function happened to be invoked. Testing the internal call instead of the outcome also makes the test brittle in the wrong direction: a legitimate refactor that computes the same correct discount a different way (without calling `_round_currency` at all) would break this test despite the actual behavior being perfectly correct — testing implementation structure instead of observable behavior.

contentSections.body: Verifying a mock was called is only meaningful when the call itself is the actual point (a real side effect that matters) — when it stands in for checking the function's real output, it can pass for a badly wrong result and break on a harmless refactor.

title: Coverage as a map of what nobody checked
description: Coverage percentage measures which lines executed during the test suite, not which lines had their behavior actually verified — the number is more reliably read backward than forward.

learningObjectives.text: Explain precisely what a coverage percentage measures and what it doesn't
Use an uncovered line as a reliable signal, and a covered line's coverage status as an unreliable one, about test quality

contentSections.title: What 'covered' actually means, mechanically

contentSections.body:
A generated PR proudly reports "98% test coverage" on a new payment-processing module. Inside that module, this exact line — from the mock-agreement scenario earlier in this module — is marked covered, green, executed:

```python
result = process_payment(order)
assert result.transaction_id == 'tx_123'
```

That line ran. The coverage tool sees it ran and marks it green. The coverage tool has no way to know, and does not check, whether the assertion beneath it was vacuous, whether the mock feeding it was shaped to agree with a bug, or whether `'tx_123'` is even a value that could plausibly differ from what a wrong implementation would also produce. "98% covered" and "98% correctly verified" are different claims, and a coverage report only makes the first one.

Code coverage is a mechanical measurement: which lines, branches, or statements were *executed* at least once while the test suite ran. That's genuinely useful information, read correctly — but 'executed' and 'checked' are different properties, and coverage tooling only measures the first one. A line can execute and be followed by an assertion that's vacuous (this module's third lesson), or by a mock so tightly shaped to the code's own assumptions that it can't disagree (the fourth lesson), and the coverage tool marks that line green regardless, because from its perspective, execution happened — it has no visibility into whether anything meaningful was verified about what happened.

This asymmetry is the single most important thing to internalize about a coverage number: an **uncovered** line is a reliable, strong signal — it means, unambiguously, that nothing in the test suite ever exercised that code path at all, full stop, no exceptions. A **covered** line is a much weaker signal — it means the line ran during some test, and says nothing about whether that test's assertions were capable of catching a wrong result if that line had produced one. Coverage percentage is far more trustworthy read as 'here is a map of what's definitely never been tested at all' than as 'here is a map of what's been properly verified.'

This matters specifically for AI-generated test suites because a high coverage number is a genuinely easy target for a model to hit — coverage-maximizing test generation, given a function, tends to produce tests that execute every branch (satisfying the coverage tool) without necessarily producing assertions specific enough to catch a wrong result on any of those branches, especially when combined with the vacuous-assertion and mirror-mock patterns from the last two lessons. A 95%+ coverage number on generated code is worth treating as 'nearly everything ran at least once,' not as 'nearly everything was actually verified.'

contentSections.scenario: A generated test suite for a 40-line pricing module reports 100% line coverage. On closer reading, 6 of its 12 tests use assertions this module's third and fourth lessons would flag as vacuous or mirror-mocked (checking `is not None`, checking a mock was called without checking the outcome, or using mock values derived from the implementation itself).
contentSections.question: Given that half the tests are weak in this specific way, what's your best guess for what percentage of this module's actual, meaningful behavioral requirements (correct values under real conditions, not just 'ran without crashing') this suite genuinely verifies — despite the 100% line-coverage number?
contentSections.explanation: There's no single correct number here, and that's the point — a reasonable estimate is well under the reported 100%, roughly in the neighborhood of what the strong half of the tests actually cover, since the weak half contributes execution (satisfying the coverage tool) without contributing much real verification. The exercise isn't about landing on an exact figure; it's about registering that '100% coverage' and 'this module's behavior is 100% verified' are simply different claims, and a large gap between them is entirely possible — even likely — in a suite where half the assertions are close to vacuous, regardless of what the coverage percentage reports.

contentSections.body: An uncovered line is a strong, reliable signal that nothing was tested there at all. A covered line only means something executed — it says nothing about whether what ran was actually checked meaningfully, which is a completely separate question the coverage tool can't see.

contentSections.title: Reading coverage alongside the assertions, not instead of them

contentSections.body:
None of this makes coverage numbers worthless — used correctly, as a map of what's definitely never been touched, a coverage report is one of the fastest ways to find the parts of a generated module that have zero test evidence behind them at all, which is exactly where to start reading the implementation cold, with none of this module's earlier head-start techniques available. The mistake is treating a high coverage number as a substitute for actually reading a sample of the assertions themselves, the way this module's third and fourth lessons practiced.

The practical habit closing this module, and this whole phase: when handed a generated PR reporting high coverage, treat the number as an invitation to sample-check, not a reason to skip reading. Pick a handful of the most consequential covered lines — the ones handling money, security, or a genuinely tricky edge case — and read their actual backing assertions with the specific, narrow-vacuous-detecting eye this module has been building. A coverage report tells you where to look for the *absence* of testing reliably. It cannot tell you, on its own, where testing that exists is actually any good.

contentSections.title: The 100% coverage report
contentSections.opening: A generated PR for a discount-code redemption feature reports 100% line and branch coverage. It's late in a sprint, everyone's tired, and the coverage badge is green.

start.situation: You're the reviewer. The coverage report is the most visible piece of evidence in the PR.
start.question: What's your first move?

choices.label: Approve based on the 100% coverage figure — full coverage on a well-scoped feature is a strong signal
choices.consequence: Two weeks later, a customer reports a discount code that should have been single-use got applied twice on the same order. The test suite's coverage was real — every line ran — but the assertion checking 'redeemed' status used `is not None` instead of checking the actual boolean value, missing the double-redemption bug entirely.

choices.label: Spend five minutes reading the actual assertions on the lines that touch money and redemption state specifically, ignoring the coverage number itself
choices.consequence: You find exactly the vacuous `is not None` assertion on the redemption-state check, before merge.

found-it.situation: You've found one vacuous assertion on a consequential line. The rest of the suite's coverage is real, but you now have reason to wonder about the rest.
found-it.question: What's the proportionate next step?

choices.label: Ask for just this one assertion to be strengthened, and approve the rest as-is based on the coverage number
choices.consequence: The fix goes in, but a second vacuous assertion elsewhere in the same suite — on a related discount-stacking check — ships unnoticed, because the review stopped after finding one.

choices.label: Use the one finding as a reason to specifically sample a few more of the money- and state-related assertions across the same suite, not just fix the one found and stop
choices.consequence: You find the second vacuous assertion on the discount-stacking check before merge, and both get fixed together.

missed.summary: A 100% coverage number was trusted as a substitute for reading assertions, and a genuinely serious bug — a discount code usable twice — shipped inside a fully green test suite.
missed.lesson: Coverage measures execution, not verification. A green coverage badge on a suite full of vacuous assertions is a confident, entirely unearned signal.

partial.summary: The one vacuous assertion that was found got fixed, but finding one weak assertion is evidence the same author's pattern likely repeats elsewhere in the same suite — and it did.
partial.lesson: One vacuous assertion found is a sample result, not a complete audit — the same weak pattern that produced it is likely to have produced others nearby, worth checking rather than assuming it was isolated.

resolved.summary: The initial finding prompted a broader, still-proportionate sample of the suite's most consequential assertions, catching a second real gap before it shipped.
resolved.lesson: A coverage number tells you where nothing was tested. Reading the actual assertions, especially once one weak pattern is found, is what tells you whether what was tested actually verifies anything — and finding one instance of a pattern is a reason to look for more, not a reason to stop.

contentSections.body: Use coverage to find what's definitely untested, then read the assertions on the most consequential covered lines directly — a coverage number alone can't tell you whether what ran was actually checked for anything real.

Identify the specific wrong result an assertion, mock, or coverage number would fail to catch

title: Lab — Review a Generated Test Suite for Tests That Cannot Fail
description: Take a real test suite and find every test that would pass regardless of whether the code is correct — then write down what should replace each one.

learningObjectives.text: Apply vacuous-assertion detection, mirror-mock detection, and coverage-reading discipline to a real test suite
Produce a review naming every vacuous test with a specific, stronger replacement assertion

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Every lesson this module worked one test-reading risk at a time. A real generated test suite usually has several of these mixed together — a genuinely solid test next to a vacuous one next to a mirror-mocked one, all reporting the same green checkmark. This lab is a full pass over one real suite, specifically hunting for every test that cannot fail, and closing this whole phase's arc: from reading a single function for intent, to tracing its control flow, to checking the shape of its data, to weighing its dependencies, to — finally — checking whether the tests that are supposed to back all of it up actually verify anything at all.

contentSections.title: Review a test suite for tests that cannot fail
contentSections.brief: Pick a real test file — from your own project, an AI-generated one you haven't scrutinized, or an open-source project's test suite — with at least eight tests covering real logic (not pure configuration or trivial getters). If nothing fits, generate a small module and its test suite now for a plausible feature (an order-total calculator, a permissions checker, a scheduling function) and treat the generated tests as your subject.
contentSections.deliverable: A review naming every test in the suite that would pass regardless of whether the underlying code is correct — vacuous assertions, mirror-mocked dependencies, or tests that only check 'didn't crash' — with the specific, stronger assertion that should replace each one.

stages.title: Map the suite and extract requirements
stages.instructions: For each test, decompose its arrangement and assertion the way this module practiced, and write down the specific requirement it appears to encode. Note where a test's name claims more than its assertion actually checks.
stages.checkpoint: Every test has a one-line extracted requirement, and any name-versus-scope gaps are flagged.

stages.title: Hunt for vacuous assertions and mirror-mocks
stages.instructions: For each assertion, ask what wrong value would still satisfy it — flag anything close to vacuous. For any mocks, trace whether their values come from a real, independent source or from the code under test itself.
stages.checkpoint: Every test is marked as either genuinely verifying something, or flagged with a specific reason it's weak — not a vague 'this seems off.'

stages.title: Write the deliverable and self-check
stages.instructions: For every flagged test, write the specific stronger assertion that should replace it — a real expected value, a check on an actual side effect rather than an internal call, or a mock value sourced correctly. Compress into the deliverable and self-check against the rubric.
stages.checkpoint: Every flagged test has a specific, concrete replacement assertion, not just a note that it's weak.

rubric.criterion: Every test in the suite is accounted for, not just a sample
rubric.meets: The review covers the whole file, even if most entries are quick 'this one's fine, here's why' notes.

rubric.criterion: Each flagged test names the specific wrong value or bug it would fail to catch
rubric.meets: The flag isn't just 'this is vacuous' — it names a concrete wrong result that would still pass.

rubric.criterion: Mirror-mocks are checked for, not just vacuous assertions
rubric.meets: Any mocked dependency has its value's source explicitly traced, even if the conclusion is 'this one is sourced correctly.'

rubric.criterion: Every flagged test has a specific replacement assertion
rubric.meets: The fix names an actual expected value or check, not a general instruction like 'make this stronger.'

rubric.criterion: The review distinguishes genuinely solid tests from flagged ones explicitly
rubric.meets: A reader can tell, for every single test, whether it passed the review or why it didn't — nothing is left ambiguous.

contentSections.body: A green test suite and a correct codebase are two different claims — the gap between them is exactly the set of tests that were never actually capable of failing, and finding them is the last, and maybe most consequential, reading skill this phase built.

description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from Dependencies and What They Cost, two from Data Shapes and Boundaries. Ungraded, untimed.

questions.from: This module — Tests as a Reading Tool
questions.prompt: Why is a passing test structurally more trustworthy than an accurate-looking comment, at the moment you read either one?

options.label: A test is re-verified every time the build runs and fails loudly if it stops being true; a comment can silently drift from the code with nothing checking it
Comments are always written before the code, while tests are always written after
Tests are shorter than comments, so they're less likely to contain an error

questions.explanation: This is the module's opening distinction — a test's relationship to ongoing truth is mechanically different from a comment's, regardless of how each currently reads.

questions.from: This module — Tests as a Reading Tool
questions.prompt: A test named `test_handles_invalid_input` asserts on exactly one malformed string. What does this test actually establish?

options.label: Only that this one specific input is handled as expected — nothing about the broader category the name implies
That the function handles all forms of invalid input correctly, since the name states it generally
That the function's error handling is broken

questions.explanation: A test's name is a claim, not a guarantee about its assertion's actual scope — one example only establishes that one example.

questions.from: This module — Tests as a Reading Tool
questions.prompt: Why is `assert result > 0` dangerous rather than just unhelpful, for a function whose bug produces a wildly inflated (but still positive) number?

options.label: Its pass condition is wide enough to include both the correct answer and a large space of badly wrong ones, so it produces a false, unearned green checkmark rather than just adding no value
It's dangerous because it will always fail even for correct code
It only becomes dangerous when combined with a try/except block

questions.explanation: The tax-calculation example showed a nearly-tenfold overcharge sailing through `result > 0` untouched — the assertion manufactures false confidence, not just a missed opportunity.

questions.from: This module — Tests as a Reading Tool
questions.prompt: What does an uncovered line in a coverage report tell you, compared to a covered line?

options.label: An uncovered line reliably means nothing was tested there at all; a covered line only means something executed, saying nothing about whether it was checked meaningfully
Both are equally reliable indicators of test quality
A covered line is always backed by a meaningful assertion, by definition of the coverage tool

questions.explanation: This asymmetry is the module's closing point — uncovered is a strong, nearly unambiguous signal; covered is a much weaker one that requires actually reading the assertion to interpret.

questions.from: Previous module — Dependencies and What They Cost
questions.prompt: Why does a model reach for a library like lodash for a task a few lines of standard-library code could handle?

options.label: It's producing the statistically common shape of code for this task from its training data — not weighing this project's specific concerns
Because dependencies always make code run faster
Because using the standard library is considered deprecated practice

questions.explanation: The `_.pick` example showed a model reaching for a familiar library out of statistical habit, not a deliberate tradeoff this specific project needed made.

questions.from: Previous module — Dependencies and What They Cost
questions.prompt: What's the mechanism that makes 'slopsquatting' a distinct risk from an ordinary malicious package upload?

options.label: The target package name is predictable in advance, because models tend to hallucinate similar plausible names repeatedly, giving an attacker a name to specifically watch for and register
It only ever affects already-popular packages
It requires guessing a common human typo

questions.explanation: The `requests_retry_toolkit` scenario showed a hallucinated name becoming a discoverable, researchable target — distinct from typosquatting's reliance on typing mistakes.

questions.from: Previous module — Dependencies and What They Cost
questions.prompt: What does the AGPL license's distinguishing clause specifically cover that GPL alone doesn't?

options.label: Software run as a network service, even when never literally distributed as a copy to users
Software installed only on a user's personal device
Internal-only developer tooling

questions.explanation: The AGPL specifically closes the network-service gap the regular GPL doesn't cover — relevant to nearly any modern SaaS product.

questions.from: Previous module — Dependencies and What They Cost
questions.prompt: What's the actual ongoing cost a project takes on the moment a new dependency is added?

options.label: A small, recurring, easy-to-forget claim on future attention — eventual upgrades, breaking-change migrations, and security response
Nothing beyond the initial install time
A one-time cost that's fully paid off once the code passes review

questions.explanation: The install is the cheapest moment in the whole relationship — the real cost is deferred and diffuse, which is exactly why it's easy to underweight during a correctness-focused review.

questions.from: Two modules back — Data Shapes and Boundaries
questions.prompt: A sensitive function has no internal validation and one currently-validated caller. What does this module say about its actual safety?

options.label: Its safety is entirely borrowed from that one caller, and remains safe only as long as every future caller independently re-implements the same checks
It's permanently safe, since the current caller was already reviewed
Validation should never happen at entry points

questions.explanation: The `process_transfer` case-sim showed a second caller reaching the same unvalidated function without the original route's checks.

questions.from: Two modules back — Data Shapes and Boundaries
questions.prompt: Why does `data as User` (a TypeScript type assertion) provide no real protection against a malformed API response?

options.label: A type assertion is a compile-time-only instruction with zero runtime effect — nothing actually inspects the real value's shape
TypeScript assertions only work for primitive types
It works fine as long as the API is generally reliable

questions.explanation: The `getUser` example traced this exactly — the assertion told the compiler to stop checking, and the resulting crash happened downstream, far from the actual mismatch.
